| Roach King | A giant cockroach appears when you have pizza and asks for some. | Let it in and sacrifice five slices of pizza. | 
Transluscent Guest
The Transluscent Guest looks like an ordinary visitor at first, but the security camera reveals that their body is see through. This visual difference is the key clue, so check the hallway camera before opening the door and lock it when you spot the Anomaly.
Doppelganger
The Doppelganger can be identified by looking for a second version of the visitor in the hallway. The copy appears slumped against the wall beside the real guest, making the security camera the safest way to spot it before opening the door.
Dead Doppelganger
The Dead Doppelganger has an even more disturbing visual clue, as a dead version of the visitor appears in the hallway. Check beside the stairs for the body on the security camera, then lock the door if you see it.
Window Seeker
The Window Seeker is identified through sounds coming from outside the hotel window, including moans, knocks, scuffling, and scratching. Open the curtains and look at the creature to force it back to its first phase, then repeat this whenever it returns.
Door Breaker
The Door Breaker is a gaunt white creature that runs toward your door while panting before attempting to force its way inside. When the game tells you to hide, get underneath the bed and wait until the creature leaves.
Spiders
Spiders can be spotted crawling across the ceiling with giant egg sacs attached to their backs. They eventually make a noise and explode, so pay attention to where they are and move away from the area underneath them to avoid taking Sanity damage.
Shadow Man
The Shadow Man appears as an ominous figure standing in a corner of your room and watching you. When you spot the dark figure, turn on your flashlight and point it at him until he disappears.
Knife Killer
The Knife Killer appears at the door carrying a knife and later creates a threat while you are preparing to sleep. If he appears that day, turn off the light before going to bed to prevent him from entering your room.
Silent Lady
The Silent Lady is a tall, gaunt woman who appears at the door and silently stares at you. Use the security cameras to look at her, which triggers a jumpscare and removes the threat.
Vent Ghost
The Vent Ghost appears when a dishevelled man drops from the vent and crawls around your room. Stand on the bed and wait for him to crawl back into the vent before continuing with your night.
The Darkness
The Darkness begins when a pair of hands covers your eyes and transports you into an endless void. Follow the lights ahead of you until you reach the doorway that returns you to the real world.
Bathroom Monster
The Bathroom Monster lives inside the bathroom and can attack you while you sleep. Make sure at least one non Anomaly resident is sleeping in your room before you go to bed to prevent the attack.
The cake is a lie
This is one of the most different Anomalies in Keep the Door Locked because the cake itself is not dangerous. If you spot a lone piece of cake sitting on a trolley outside your door, open the door to eat it and recover Sanity.
Hacked laptop
The Hacked laptop prevents you from accessing the security cameras by displaying a message saying the device has been hacked. You need to pay $300 to decode the laptop and regain access to the cameras.
Spasming limbs
Spasming limbs is easy to recognize when a visitor arrives with their arms and legs flailing uncontrollably. The unusual movement is the giveaway, so lock the door rather than allowing this visitor inside.
Long limbs
Long limbs is identified through the visitor’s unusually extended arms. Check the security camera for the abnormal body shape, then lock the door when you confirm the Anomaly.
Neck Craner
The Neck Craner arrives with its neck bent backward while staring toward the ceiling. This unnatural pose makes the visitor easy to distinguish through the camera, and you should lock the door when you spot it.
Room Hider
The Room Hider appears somewhere inside your room rather than waiting outside the door. Look around carefully for the hidden figure, then look directly at it to trigger a jumpscare and make it leave.
Headbanger
The Headbanger can be recognized when a visitor violently smashes their head against your door. When the quick time event appears, complete it to drive the Anomaly away from the door.
Roach King
The Roach King is a giant cockroach that appears at your door when you have pizza in the room and asks for some food. Let it inside, and it will eat five slices before leaving; refusing it causes a swarm of normal cockroaches to enter the room.
That completes the list of all Anomalies from Keep the Door Locked. Did you encounter all of them yet? Tell us in the comments.
How do I identify Anomalies in Keep the Door Locked?
Check the security camera and look for unusual features that separate the visitor from regular guests.
How many Anomalies are there in Keep the Door Locked?
There are currently 20 Anomalies to identify in the game.

Tielemans apologises to Villa fans for Man Utd remarks
- Published
Youri Tielemans has apologised to Aston Villa fans after suggesting he had moved to a bigger club in Premier League rivals Manchester United.
The Belgium midfielder, 29, moved to Old Trafford this summer on a five-year deal from Villa when United triggered a £35m release clause in his contract.
Tielemans spent three years at Villa Park after joining from Leicester City in 2023, making 134 appearances and scoring 10 goals.
Speaking during United's pre-season tour, Tielemans praised Villa for putting him "back to my best level", before adding: "But there are clubs above Villa, and Manchester United is one of them."
Some Villa fans were unhappy with Tielemans' comments, so he took to Instagram, external to clear the air.
"Never meant for my words in the press yesterday to offend anyone or the institution of Aston Villa Football Club, which I massively respect and I'm grateful for the past 3 years," he wrote on Thursday.
"I must however admit my mistake and apologise for my choice of words, will be more careful in the future.
"Wishing the club the best in the future."
- I owe Villa the world but Man Utd are above them - Tielemans 
  - Published1 day ago
Tielemans, who helped Belgium reach the quarter-finals of the World Cup this summer, signed for United in July until 2031.
Last season he suffered separate calf and ankle problems that restricted him to 35 appearances in all competitions for Villa, the lowest number in a campaign during his time in England.
He called his move to Old Trafford "the culmination of years of dedication since I first fell in love with football" and said signing for "such a special club" like United "feels incredible".
United take on AC Milan and Villa face Borussia Monchengladbach in their final pre-season games on Saturday, before the new Premier League campaign begins next weekend.

Twenty-eight-year-old Jacob Fortinsky has been busy. “I was a groomsman at two weddings this weekend,” he tells me over Zoom. Also, the sports trading company he runs, Novig, launched its prediction market last week, facilitating $18 million in trading volume on its first day. Today, Novig launches a “responsible trading framework” in its exchange rulebook, codifying its guardrails as part of its effort to be seen as a kinder, gentler prediction market player.
Unlike industry leaders like Polymarket and Kalshi, which allow people 18 and older to participate, you have to be at least 21 to use Novig. Fortinsky says that decision was made in response to “valid concerns” put forth about the susceptibility of younger participants to risky behavior, including lobbying from the NCAA and other professional groups. Fortinsky sees this move as staying ahead of the curve as concerns grow about the negative impact that prediction markets can have on teens. “There’s a broader reckoning coming with the younger traders,” he says. “That group is particularly susceptible to irresponsible behavior and financial ruin.”
Novig’s rulebook also prohibits marketing to minors, and lays out guidelines banning other marketing practices, like ads that claim there’s no risk or ads that try to appeal to a prospective participant’s money troubles. That means when it advertises on TikTok, for example, it uses a setting that allows targeting only people over 21. Fortinsky positions these restrictions as part of Novig’s push to be seen as a “serious, legitimate financial product” as it comes onto the scene. “Some of our competitors, I think, have been seen as being a little bit more cavalier in certain regards,” he says. (He declined to name specific rivals.)
Because Novig only offers sports-themed markets, it doesn’t wade into some of the more hotly contested topics, like US elections and the Iran war. That doesn’t mean it’s avoiding controversy. As a sports-centered platform, the types of speculation opportunities it offers are at the center of an ongoing regulatory war, with prediction markets and federal regulators on one side and state regulators, tribal authorities, and occasionally traditional sportsbooks and casino operators on the other. Dozens of messy legal battles are raging across the US. States are suing Kalshi and other platforms, alleging that they illegally offer gambling; Kalshi is suing right back; the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees the industry, is suing several states, arguing that it alone has jurisdiction over these markets.
Also, Novig isn’t immune to the general cultural distaste for prediction markets; when the New York Mets announced a recent partnership with Novig, the baseball team received a flood of criticism on social media. Sample post: “This is vile.”
If sports-related event contracts offered by prediction markets are banned, big players like Kalshi and Polymarket will be in deep trouble, with the majority of the action on their services gone. But Novig’s position is even shakier, since that’s all it does.
Fortinsky is betting it all on a win, and Novig wasted no time jumping into the legal fray. Within three days of launching, the startup sued New York, Massachusetts, New Mexico, and Washington, all states that have taken an aggressive approach to curbing prediction markets. It is trying to block these states from attempting to apply their gambling laws to federally regulated exchanges, which is what it’s licensed as. Sports betting attorney Daniel Wallach tells WIRED that these complaints are a “great marketing strategy” and a way to announce that Novig has arrived on the scene.
Whether they'll be successful is another matter. Recent court decisions have largely swung toward state attorneys general. A judge in New York denied Novig’s efforts to get a temporary restraining order, on the grounds that doing so would undermine another decision already reached in a case against Kalshi. “It’s increasingly looking more positive for the states,” Wallach notes. But that could change; Wallach and other onlookers expect the fight to get kicked up to the US Supreme Court before anything is definitively resolved.
Until then, Novig is plowing ahead. One of Novig’s appeals to customers is that it offers a different kind of sports speculation experience, one without a house that takes a “vig,” the fee that bookies take for arranging a bet. (“No vig,” get it?) Fortinsky has harsh words for many of the dominant sports gambling players, calling sportsbooks “inefficient, exploitative, and predatory.” He sees the peer-to-peer model that prediction markets facilitate as distinct, since it’s two parties on equal footing going up directly against each other. But if Novig goes how he’d like it to go, those parties won’t always be two average sports fans squaring off. The company is actively courting financial institutions to take sides of wagers, and Fortinsky says Novig is currently onboarding proprietary trading firms and banks. The company is taking steps to make it easier to “trade programmatically,” using algorithms to automate placing money on which team will win the Super Bowl or how many times the Mets will lose, for example.
“Something that's really cool to see,” he says, “is that you have hundreds of these small shops with a couple guys with $100,000 that are now competing against some of the largest Wall Street trading firms in the world and doing quite well.” Good thing the teens aren’t allowed in.

Larsen & Toubro (L&T) is consolidating its data centre, cloud and AI infrastructure businesses under newly incorporated subsidiary Vyoma.AI as it bids to build a larger play in India’s fast-growing AI infrastructure market. Earlier this week, L&T transferred its data centre and cloud services business to Vyoma for ₹1,400 Cr. Today, the conglomerate said Vyoma’s AI infrastructure subsidiary, LTN Compute, has secured an order from US-based AI cloud platform Together AI to deploy an AI factory at L&T’s Chennai data centre. The facility is expected to house 10,000 NVIDIA B300 GPUs, with 8,000 GPUs forming one cluster under its agreement with Together AI and another 2,000 GPUs being deployed as a separate cluster to serve customers. The two developments are in line with the conglomerate's envisioned scale of ambitions for Vyoma, which is looking to move beyond conventional data centre operations into a full-stack digital infrastructure business spanning colocation, cloud and AI factories. Speaking to Inc42, Vyoma MD Prashant Chiranjive Jain outlined the company’s strategy to build out this stack as demand for compute, power and connectivity accelerates. From Data Centres To AI Factories Being a construction behemoth, L&T’s initial data centre strategy was built around owning and operating colocation infrastructure. The company, however, soon realised that it needed to move up the AI value chain. For this, adding public, private and sovereign cloud services to its offerings seemed the pressing need. Founded in 2024, Vyoma was initially incorporated as L&T Cloudfiniti — an incubated new-age business subsidiary. It was rebranded as Vyoma.AI a year later as L&T broadened its focus towards AI-enabled digital infrastructure. Today, Vyoma’s business is built around three pillars — colocation, cloud and AI factories. Its cloud business includes public, private and sovereign cloud offerings, while the company is also developing its own cloud IP, Jain said. The company has already begun building a sovereign AI infrastructure stack, aimed at giving enterprises a secure environment to deploy CPU and GPU compute without moving sensitive data to public AI platforms. L&T’s data centre journey began with a 2 MW pilot facility in Panvel, followed by a 30 MW facility in Chennai. The Chennai campus currently has 150 MVA of live power and can support up to 250 MW of capacity. L&T is now converting a large part of that infrastructure for AI workloads. Of the existing 30 MW facility, around 6 MW will continue to operate as a colocation facility, while the remaining 24 MW is being converted into what the company calls an ‘AI mega factory’. L&T expects the B300-powered AI factory to go live by November, while continuing to operate NVIDIA H100, H200 and B200 GPUs at its Chennai facility. The company plans to deploy next-generation Vera Rubin and Blackwell platforms at subsequent facilities. The scale of the planned infrastructure is significant. Jain said the current NVIDIA-linked AI factory represents around 23 MW of AI infrastructure. “The capex investment we have set for the current setup and the expansion is roughly ₹10,000-12,000 Cr earmarked, which includes the existing data centre and kickstarting the expansion,” he said. The company is also looking beyond Chennai. With land, power and permits already available, L&T is evaluating the next phase of expansion at the campus. Meanwhile, L&T has broken ground on a potential second data centre campus in Mahape, Maharashtra. Jain said the company is evaluating two facilities with capacity of around 40 MW each, with the overall campus potentially scaling up to 100 MW. L&T is also in discussions with multiple state governments to secure additional land parcels for future data centre development. However, Jain said land availability is not the biggest constraint at present. “The constraint is deploying sovereign scale technology and getting it up and running. That is what we are focusing on,” Jain said. For context, AI data centres require higher power density and more sophisticated cooling and networking infrastructure than conventional facilities. For instance, L&T’s existing Chennai facility was initially designed for rack densities of around 12.5 kW. As the company began deploying H100 and H200 GPUs, it had to retrofit parts of the facility to accommodate higher-density AI workloads. Jain sees the emerging AI infrastructure market as an ecosystem rather than a winner-takes-all contest, with different players operating across the infrastructure, compute and software layers. “At the bottom is the physical infrastructure layer — land, power, permits, cooling and storage. Above that sits the compute layer, comprising CPUs and GPUs, followed by networking, cybersecurity and other software layers,” he said. This layered architecture also allows Vyoma to target different customer segments. While Hyperscalers and neoclouds can use its physical infrastructure to deploy their own compute, other customers can check out the underlying cloud or AI stack. Some can also opt for a fully managed solution. “Some are deploying an asset-light model and would want somebody else to provide the data centre. Somebody would need just the stack, and somebody needs the solution wrapped,” Jain said. E2E Strategic Investment L&T is also building out its AI infrastructure business through strategic investments and partnerships. In 2024, the company announced an investment of approximately ₹1,407 Cr to acquire a minority stake of up to 21% in listed AI and hyperscale cloud platform provider E2E Networks. To note, Jain sits on E2E's board as a non-executive, non-independent director. The partnership combines L&T’s data centre footprint with E2E’s GPU-powered cloud infrastructure. E2E is also operating the 2,000 B200 GPUs deployed at the Chennai facility. Jain said these GPUs are being operated by E2E for client workloads, while the larger 10,000-GPU B300 deployment will be operated by Vyoma as its own AI factory. L&T’s Larger Pivot To Emerging Tech Vyoma's incorporation comes as L&T looks to expand beyond its traditional infrastructure and engineering businesses into technology-led growth areas. Jain, who has been with L&T since 2024, was initially roped into L&T to work on future technology businesses and is responsible for the innovation fund, data centre business and electronics products and systems (EPS). As the data centre and EPS businesses moved out of incubation and received capex approvals, Jain handed over the innovation fund and took charge of the data centre business as MD, while continuing to head EPS. For Vyoma, the immediate priority is to scale the infrastructure already under development. The longer-term ambition, however, is to combine L&T’s traditional strengths in infrastructure, construction and project execution with the growing demand for compute, cloud and AI.

Din, disruptions and a dozen bills: Monsoon Session comes to a close
The disruptions had two key flashpoints. One was the police crackdown on students at Jantar Mantar and the other was the alleged theft of Ram Temple donations.
Parliament's 25-day monsoon session ended in acrimony on Thursday, with both Houses adjourned sine die after a stretch that saw proceedings disrupted almost daily, with Lok Sabha going without a completed Question Hour on even a single sitting day.
The disruptions had two key flashpoints. One was the July 20 police crackdown on students protesting at Jantar Mantar over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak — an episode that led to Dharmendra Pradhan’s resignation as Union education minister, and that the opposition wanted Union home minister Amit Shah to explain in the House.
The other was a running opposition allegation of theft of donations collected at the Ram temple in Ayodhya.
The Lok Sabha played all six stanzas of the national song Vande Mataram soon after convening on Thursday, after which speaker Om Birla adjourned the House sine die. He skipped the traditional valedictory address, which typically highlights the session's performance and productivity. The Congress, the Samajwadi Party and the Trinamool Congress boycotted the customary meeting with Birla thereafter.
Also Read | Lok Sabha Om Birla urges Opposition to end Parliament logjam
The Rajya Sabha was also adjourned sine die, ending the session. Chairman CP Radhakrishnan expressed "deep concern" over disruptions that "derailed" the business of the House. Overall, the Lok Sabha functioned for 17.5 hours while the Rajya Sabha worked for 37.4 hours.
Jantar Mantar crackdown dominates session
The session was dominated by a showdown between the Opposition and the Centre over the former's demand for a debate and a statement by Shah on the police crackdown on protesting students at Delhi's Jantar Mantar last month, which led to the resignation of Dharmendra Pradhan as Union education minister.
On the penultimate day, the Centre's push for a debate failed as the Opposition rejected Shah's offer of a two-day discussion on the NEET paper leak and other issues, followed by a reply from him. "The Centre is ready for discussions. The House should be allowed to run, the Opposition should submit a letter to the speaker by 2pm today. We are ready to start discussion at 3pm today," Shah told reporters outside Parliament on Wednesday.
Also Read | Rijiju defends Shah amid Oppn persistent demand for HM’s statement
He also wrote to Birla conveying the government's readiness to participate in the discussion. Congress leader Rahul Gandhi called it a “last-minute attempt” and said the Opposition was not interested in listening to Shah’s lecture.
The bills Parliament dealt with
Despite repeated disruptions and protests inside and outside Parliament, both Houses tabled and in some cases, passed a series of bills.
Foreign contribution bill referred to JPC after Opposition, church pushback
A bill proposing contentious changes to India's foreign contribution law was referred to a 31-member joint parliamentary committee (JPC) amid a standoff between the government and the Opposition, and repeated disruptions in the Lok Sabha on Wednesday.
Among the key concerns are a plan to empower a "designated authority" to take over, manage or sell assets built with foreign funds by non-governmental organisations whose licences are cancelled, suspended or not renewed.
The Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill - it was introduced in the previous session but held back - drew objections from the Opposition, several church delegations and four chief ministers of Christian-majority states.
Minister of state for home affairs Nityanand Rai moved the resolution in the Lok Sabha to form the JPC, comprising 21 Lok Sabha members and 10 Rajya Sabha members. A BJP member is expected to head the panel. The Opposition, which had pushed the government to scrap the bill, said it would join the committee.
Centre, Opposition united over paper leak
The Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Amendment Bill, 2026 — brought against the backdrop of protests by students after the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak — was the only legislation passed in both Houses after a full debate this session. The bill overhauls the 2024 law by introducing stricter jail terms, enhancing penalties, and setting timelines for probe and trial in fast-track courts.
According to PRS Legislative Research, the Lok Sabha spent over 10 hours discussing the bill and the Rajya Sabha over six hours. Opposition parties led by the Congress staged a walkout before the bill was passed in the Rajya Sabha, with leader of the Opposition Mallikarjun Kharge saying it was incomplete in its current form. Leader of the House JP Nadda condemned the move.
"It is indeed an achievement to clear a number of bills with one week left in the session. But we should not be blamed for passing the bills amid din," a senior government functionary told HT on condition of anonymity.
New law brings banking records into the digital age
Both Houses passed the Bankers' Books Evidence Bill, 2026, replacing a 135-year-old British-era statute with a framework that makes electronic, digital, virtual and cloud-stored bank records admissible and enforceable evidence in court.
The law it replaces, the Bankers' Books Evidence Act of 1891, was built for a world of physical ledgers, and was never designed for cloud-based, electronic, digital or other storage formats even after several amendments.
Delayed registration of births, deaths made more stringent
Parliament also passed the Registration of Births and Deaths (Amendment) Bill, tightening one of India's oldest civil laws. The change is narrow on paper — a single sub-section of the Registration of Births and Deaths Act, 1969 — but it re-routes how births and deaths reported more than two years late are registered.
Beyond that threshold, cases now go to a judicial magistrate of the first class, a judicial officer under the high court, instead of an executive magistrate, a district-cadre administrator under the state government.
This is the second time in three years that Parliament has amended a statute most people encounter only once — to prove they were born.
"The government wants that every child born in the country should be registered and every death should also be registered... Anyone who has died, cannot continue to remain in the voter lists to benefit some parties," minister of state for home affairs Nityanand Rai said.
Several members of the National Democratic Alliance backed the bill as necessary, while the Opposition pressed for Shah's presence in the House. CPI(M)'s AA Rahim, among those raising the demand, cited the deaths of more than 20 students linked to the NEET paper leak.
'Vande Mataram' gets legal protection on a par with national anthem
Both Houses cleared a bill giving Vande Mataram the same legal status as the national anthem — the first bill passed amid din this session. President Droupadi Murmu gave her assent on Tuesday.
The Prevention of Insults to National Honour (Amendment) Bill, 2026 went through on a voice vote after 14 minutes of debate, with only three MPs — DMK's K Kanimozhi and A Raja, and BJP's Sambit Patra — speaking.
It makes insulting or obstructing the national song a criminal offence, punishable by up to three years in jail and a fine, extending protections currently reserved for the national flag, anthem and Constitution.
Patra said the timing coincided with Vande Mataram's 150th anniversary. The Opposition said nationalism cannot be legislated. The move follows the Centre's earlier decision making all six stanzas mandatory, departing from the two-stanza version adopted as the national song in 1950.
Sitharaman assures no UPI tax, but bill gives Centre power to redefine what stays free
Parliament passed the Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Bill, with finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman ruling out any tax on UPI. Digital payments stay free for consumers, she said.
Cleared by the Lok Sabha last week, the bill was passed in the Rajya Sabha by a voice vote after a brief debate and Sitharaman's reply. It severs the link between the Payment and Settlement Systems Act and the Income Tax Act, and gives the government legal backing to alter the zero-MDR framework for UPI and RuPay.
Banks and payment providers cannot currently charge users on UPI or RuPay debit transactions, directly or indirectly. The bill lets the Centre decide, by notification, which payment modes stay free.
Supreme Court judges to increase
Parliament also passed the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026, raising the top court's sanctioned strength from 34 to 38 judges, including the Chief Justice of India.
The bill, which replaced a May ordinance, received the President's assent on Tuesday and comes amid a mounting case backlog. It cleared on a voice vote as Opposition members walked out, with Union minister Arjun Ram Meghwal saying the government was committed to judicial independence.
Kerala set for a new name: Keralam
Kerala will soon be known as Keralam. The Rajya Sabha passed the Kerala (Alteration of Name) Bill, 2026, by voice vote on Wednesday, a day after the Lok Sabha cleared it.
"The bill provides that the State of Kerala will be known as the State of Keralam," Rai said. The Constitution's First Schedule will be amended under Article 3 to reflect the new name.
Parliament clips states' powers to tax minerals
Parliament also passed the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, curbing states' powers to tax mineral rights and "mineral-bearing lands". The bill went through on a voice vote, without debate, amid Opposition protests.
A new section bars states from imposing "any tax, cess or such other levy (by whatever name called)" on mineral rights or mineral-bearing lands — whether linked to mineral quantity, value or royalty — unless the central government prescribes otherwise. It will take effect once the President gives assent.
Parliament passes bill to fix delayed payments to MSMEs
Parliament passed the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) Development (Amendment) Bill, 2026, aimed at the long-standing problem of delayed payments to MSMEs. The bill seeks to improve the sector's administrative structure and streamline payment mechanisms.

Anthropic investors expect the AI startup to float at a valuation of $2 trillion or more in October, a dizzying figure that would eclipse SpaceX and make the AI lab’s debut the largest-ever initial public offering.
Half a dozen of the company’s backers told the FT that Anthropic’s rapidly rising revenue would enable it to more than double its current valuation in a planned autumn float.
A listing at that level could unlock billions of dollars in gains for the five-year-old company’s early investors but would also test public markets that are growing more nervous about the AI boom.
Anthropic’s backers say booming demand for the lab’s advanced AI models and tools justifies their lofty expectations. Investors expect the Claude maker’s annualized revenue to be between $100 billion and $120 billion by the end of 2026—using the startup’s preferred measure, which infers full-year sales from recent performance—up by more than 10 times over the course of 2026.
“If Anthropic is growing 800 percent a year, you’d think at the incredibly low end they would trade at 30 times [revenue],” said one investor in the group. “That would make them a $3 trillion company.”
Anthropic lacks a publicly listed US peer that would provide a benchmark for its valuation. But companies that are seen as AI beneficiaries, such as data intelligence group Palantir and cloud company Nebius, have traded this year at roughly 55 times revenue.
Several investors said senior Anthropic executives had yet to fix the valuation target for the IPO, even in private conversations. But investors have built their own financial models.
Their bullish projections come despite mounting challenges, including rising competition from Chinese rivals, pressure for AI regulation, and a simmering feud with the US government.
Those concerns, particularly the Commerce Department’s temporary ban on Anthropic’s best models, contributed to overall revenue growth slowing in the month of June, according to two investors with knowledge of the matter. Even so, they said the company had rebounded and continued to grow at an extraordinary rate even by Silicon Valley standards.

U.S. ambassador calls settler siege of Palestinian homes a 'horrific act of terror'
JERUSALEM — The U.S. Ambassador to Israel condemned the actions of Jewish settlers who are besieging the home of an American Palestinian family in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
U.S. Ambassador Mike Huckabee called the siege a "horrific act of terror."
Since Sunday, according to local officials and family members, settlers have gathered near the home in the village of Qusra and harassed those inside, defying efforts by the Israeli military to defuse the situation.
A group that has included up to dozens of men has thrown stones, attempted to bring down a stone wall nearby, and prevented the occupants from leaving despite dwindling supplies.
Speaking to The Associated Press by phone from his home in Ohio, the home's owner Lou Ridi said his 48-year-old brother and nephew, who have been holed up in the home to defend it, had been unable to leave the house and did not have access to food or water for several days.
On Thursday morning, the owner's brother Qusai Abu Rida said that he and his teenage son had been evacuated by Israel's military. It was unclear what would happen to the property and at least one other that has been targeted.
Israeli troops intervened in recent days to try to restore order. The military said that overnight Thursday its troops had dismantled "two illegal outposts" on the outskirts of Qusra and a nearby village, and detained one Israeli. It added that additional soldiers had surged to the area, which is about 16 kilometers (10 miles) of the Palestinian city of Nablus, to "carry out defensive missions and patrols."
Journalists on the outskirts of Qusra said roads into the village were closed. Israeli police did not immediately respond to questions about whether any Israeli civilians had been arrested.
Palestinians and the Israeli opposition accuse Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's hardline government of turning a blind eye to attacks by settlers against Palestinians as clashes have surged in the last few years.
Huckabee's post on X was an unusually sharp rebuke from a U.S. official, even as he defended the Israeli military's response. Huckabee is a longtime ally of Israel's settler movement and in the past has expressed support for Israeli control over the occupied West Bank while condemning settler violence.
Home security footage from Thursday morning appeared to show a few settlers still hiding by a damaged stone wall near the house.
Ridi said that settlers have been harassing his home for months before the situation escalated in recent days, saying they had cut off the water and electricity to his house and thrown stones, causing damage to the property as well as at least one more house in the area.
"We are prisoners in our own house, hostages in our own house," he said.
Last month, a mosque in Qusra was set on fire in another apparent settler attack. That followed the killing of an Israeli settler, which triggered violence that left two Israeli soldiers and four Palestinian villagers dead.
Settlers have been building more outposts in an effort condemned by many in the international community as aimed at dismantling any remaining hopes of establishing a Palestinian state in the occupied West Bank.
The Palestinians seek the West Bank, captured by Israel in the 1967 war, as part of a future state. Many settlers and their supporters say the entire area should belong to Israel for historical, religious and security reasons.

Navi Mumbai: The growing differences between the BJP and the Shiv Sena (Shinde faction) over cluster redevelopment in CIDCO-developed colonies came to the fore during the Navi Mumbai Municipal Corporation (NMMC) General Body meeting, with the civic body passing a resolution seeking a review of the Unified Development Control and Promotion Regulations (UDCPR) and temporarily halting further action on the cluster proposal for the Simplex Colony in Ghansoli.
The confrontation was expected after Forest Minister Ganesh Naik had publicly opposed the implementation of cluster redevelopment in CIDCO-developed colony areas. The issue had been flagged ahead of the General Body meeting and has now resulted in an open political face-off between the two ruling allies.
Naik has maintained that cluster redevelopment should not be imposed in CIDCO-developed colonies and has also raised concerns over increased FSI for the redevelopment of dangerous and dilapidated buildings. His stand has brought the BJP and Shinde Sena on opposing sides, as the state government under Deputy Chief Minister and Urban Development Minister Eknath Shinde had approved increased FSI and the cluster redevelopment policy to facilitate redevelopment.
During the meeting, BJP Leader of the House Sagar Naik reiterated that the party was not opposed to redevelopment but objected to the blanket implementation of UDCPR and unnecessary cluster redevelopment. He warned that indiscriminate implementation of the regulations could put additional pressure on the infrastructure of Navi Mumbai.
“We will not allow the development of Navi Mumbai to be compromised,” Sagar Naik said, stressing the need to reconsider the UDCPR before proceeding with cluster redevelopment.
The General Body subsequently resolved to send a representation to the state government seeking reconsideration of the UDCPR. It also decided to suspend further action on cluster redevelopment until the government takes a decision. The resolution has temporarily stalled the proposed cluster redevelopment of the Simplex Colony in Ghansoli.
The Shinde Sena strongly opposed the BJP’s position, accusing the ruling party of adopting a biased approach that would adversely affect Mathadi workers. Shinde Sena corporators maintained that the redevelopment of the colony should not be obstructed and reiterated their support for the UDCPR and the state government’s redevelopment policy.
The debate saw sharp exchanges between corporators from the two parties. Local corporators Dipali Sakpal and Vaishali Maskar demanded that hurdles in the redevelopment of the Mathadi workers’ colony be removed.
Shinde Sena corporator Kishor Patkar warned that the ruling side would be responsible if an accident occurred in the ageing colony.
Opposition leader Vijay Chougule alleged that the ruling party was deliberately obstructing the redevelopment proposal and warned that such opposition would not be tolerated.
BJP corporator Suraj Patil clarified that the BJP’s opposition was not to redevelopment but to what it termed an unnecessary cluster approach.
Also Watch:
The latest confrontation reflects the widening differences between the BJP and Shinde Sena over Navi Mumbai’s redevelopment policy. While the Shinde Sena is defending the state government’s decision to promote cluster redevelopment and increased FSI to address dangerous buildings, the BJP is seeking restrictions on cluster implementation in CIDCO-developed colonies.
With the General Body resolution now before the state government, the government’s response is expected to determine the future course of the Simplex redevelopment proposal as well as the larger political and policy dispute over cluster redevelopment in Navi Mumbai.

Sonam Wangchuk's pitch for India's '2nd Independence movement' to 'reform political system'
Sonam Wangchuk has called for India's second independence movement to bring about changes in how India chooses its leaders
Scientist and activist Sonam Wangchuk has called for “India’s second Independence movement” to bring about changes in how the country chooses its leaders, urging citizens to suggest “selfless, fearless” people of character and substance who can help shape India’s future.
In a post on X on Thursday, Wangchuk said India needs a “peaceful revolution”, particularly in the way political leaders are chosen, if the country is to remain a “respectable nation” by 2047.
He highlighted the criminal cases against elected representatives, saying that close to half of India’s MPs have criminal cases against them, while a third face serious charges such as murder, rape and kidnapping. He said this was contributing to a growing “trust deficit” in the country.
Wangchuk said he wanted to consult some of the “best minds” across India to brainstorm about what needs to change and how such changes could be brought about. However, he stressed that the conversation should not be limited to intellectuals.
Instead, he called for the involvement of “selfless, fearless men and women of character and substance” who could contribute meaningfully to the effort to reform the political system.
Wangchuk, who is based in Ladakh, acknowledged that he did not know where such people could be found across the country and sought the public’s help in identifying them. He asked people to propose at least one such person from India as well as from their own region.
“Together, can we start India’s 2nd Independence movement?” he asked, framing the initiative as a collective effort to rethink the country’s political system and leadership ahead of 2047, the centenary of India’s Independence.

His wedding guests gave $6k to fund a health startup. Now it's won a $3 million prize
In 2007, Dr. Raj Panjabi, a physician at Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston, traveled to Liberia, where he was born. He had just been married and brought the $6,000 he had raised from wedding guests to help co-found a health initiative to provide care to those who lived in the country's most remote, inaccessible regions. The organization's name, Last Mile Health (LMH), reflected its mission: the belief that no one should be beyond the reach of life-saving medical help.
Today, Last Mile Health is receiving an honor that comes with a $3 million gift. It's the Conrad N. Hilton Humanitarian Prize, the world's largest humanitarian award to a nonprofit group. It's a resounding affirmation of how a group that started very small can go on to, according to the Hilton honor announcement, make extraordinary contributions toward alleviating human suffering.
But how did they reach that last mile, when physicians, nurses and medical supplies were, if available at all, scarce and far away? By using community health workers.
These are individuals who typically have a primary school education. During their eight weeks of training, they learn to diagnose and treat preventable diseases in children, including malaria, pneumonia and diarrhea, as well as help pregnant mothers develop a birth plan to deliver in the clinics. The health workers are also trained to monitor any signs of new diseases or outbreaks.
The initial $6,000 raised to start the organization served to pay the organization's first 17 workers. Since then, the group has expanded its scope with funding from governments as well as philanthropic and nonprofit institutions. In 2010, LMH began caring for HIV/AIDS patients in 12 of Liberia's 15 counties, partnering with the Government of Liberia and the Global Fund to Fight Aids, Tuberculosis and Malaria.
During the 2014-16 Ebola epidemic in Liberia, LMH trained more than 1,300 community health workers to help contain the outbreak's spread. During the COVID-19 pandemic, LMH delivered 6.2 million pieces of personal protective equipment. Going door to door to persuade people to get vaccinated, they helped lead Liberia, one of the poorest countries in the world, to an 81% vaccination rate.
Today, LMH supports 20,000 community health workers helping 32 million people not only in Liberia but in Ethiopia, Malawi and Sierra Leone. The nonprofit group has helped design a digital training program as well.
But many people who live in remote areas struggle to find medical services, points out LMH chief executive officer Lisha McCormick.
"Last Mile Health's work feels especially pressing today," Peter Laugharn, president and CEO of the Hilton Foundation, said in a statement. "Health systems in the hardest-to-reach regions still face enormous strain, and Last Mile Health has met that challenge head-on."
Panjabi, who is now president emeritus of LMH, agrees.
"We are at an unprecedented moment in global health," he says, citing projections that there could be millions more deaths by 2030 if current funding trends continue, with major reductions by the United States as well as some European countries. The projections come from a study published in Lancet , which found that U.S. foreign aid cuts in the year 2025 could lead to more than 14 million additional deaths globally by 2030, including more than 4.5 million children under five.
"Everyone wants to cut healthcare costs," he continues. "We cannot cut funds without cutting care, unless you get ahead of the disease. One of the most effective ways to get ahead of disease is to detect it at the earliest possible time. And community health workers are part of the answer."
Research exists to back the contention that beyond saving lives, community health workers also save money. A 2025 analysis of 255 studies published in SSRN, a platform for researchers from academia and, in this case, members of leading health groups like the Clinton initiative, found that more than 80% of the time, these professionals delivered care at a median cost of just $0.59 per person per year. "Overall, a decade of data shows that CHWs [community health workers] are a proven, cost-effective platform for primary health care," the paper's authors concluded.
That achievement is reflected in the experience of Genesis Whegelee, who has worked as a community health worker in Rivercess County, Liberia, since 2018.
"There was a lot of malaria, and we didn't know why children were dying in the community," he says. "Now everyone is getting [medical] attention."
Whegelee is responsible for visiting 42 households — three a day in rotation –- to assess their healthcare needs. He carries a small bag of medications and what the group calls a "job aid" –- essentially a medical textbook he can consult as he tracks the health and well-being of each family.
These visits include checking to see if there are any ill children or newly pregnant women, along with education about mosquito nets and sanitation. They account for about four hours each day. He is on call at his home the rest of the day not only doing necessary planning and paperwork but also available for emergency calls and visits.
He tells of a mother who carried her 22-month old baby from her farm to his home for an emergency visit, crying that her child was dying. "The baby was weak and feverish," Whegelee says. He gave the baby a sponge bath to bring down the fever and gave a rapid diagnostic test to see if the baby had malaria, which was the case. He then started the baby on two medications to treat it, one for malaria and the other to control the fever, and taught the mother how to continue the medication. He made follow-up visits to the child's home every day for the next five days. If the child had not improved, Whegelee would have referred her to a clinic. But in this case, "the child was better, and the mother is so happy that whenever I visit now the mother gives me a hug," Whegelee says.
Shortly before he spoke to NPR, Whegelee did have to take a child to a clinic. "The child was vomiting and had diarrhea and could not keep anything down. We were taught that is a dangerous sign. That cannot be treated at home. You cannot delay," he says.
On another occasion, he had to persuade a pregnant woman that she should deliver the baby at the hospital rather than at home in case there were complications. At first the husband was skeptical; he thought people got sick at the hospital. Whegelee succeeded in convincing the dad as well as the mom. She had trusted his advice, and the father was happy. In the routine family visits that followed, he encouraged breastfeeding and vaccines for the baby.
Such stories give support to Panjabi's belief that "The first line of contact to the health care system is often the community health worker, the neighbor trained to be one."
As for the Hilton Foundation grant, he said, "We will put the money to work immediately in the countries we currently work in now," with the goal of reaching 50 million people there by 2028. LMH will also continue to work with the continent-wide initiative it co-founded, Africa Frontline First, to introduce and implement community health worker programs to additional communities and countries.
"The community health worker model is not new, but LMH is helping professionalize them. They are not volunteers but front-line practitioners who provide diagnostic and curative services," McCormick says. She, like Panjabi, is fond of saying "Illness is universal, and access to health care is not." That is why LMH exists, she adds, "to put a health worker in reach of everyone, everywhere."
Diane Cole writes for many publications, including The Wall Street Journal and The Washington Post. She is the author of the memoir After Great Pain: A New Life Emerges. Her website is DianeJoyceCole.com

Instagram has unveiled a new wordmark, moving away from the recognizable cursive typeface it’s used over the last decade. The updated wordmark is a strange mix of half-cursive half-print that’s somehow less legible than its predecessor. Like, that totally says “Instagzam”, right?
This is Instagram’s new logo
It’s the first change to Instagram’s wordmark in a decade.
“The wordmark at the top of the app hasn’t changed in 10 years, so it was time for a refresh,” Instagram head Adam Mosseri announced on his account. “Cleaner and more modern, with references to the original and the simplicity and craft that’s always made it Instagram.”
Mosseri is seemingly aware that this will be a controversial change, because he also posted it to his Threads account to “see what the hot takes might be.” Plenty of Instagram and Threads commenters have already flagged that the updated version looks like it says “Instagzam,” but the general consensus otherwise is difficult to parse. Some users are mourning the loss of the now iconic cursive wordmark, while other responses — many of which look suspiciously written by bots — are a jumble of positive affirmations and emoji-vomit.
I don’t personally think it has the same charm, but i’ll leave the rest of you to be the judge of that.

It’s time for Rivian’s changeover from model year 2026 to 2027, and the electric vehicle startup has decided to take a page from its recently released R2 SUV and apply it to the company’s larger, more expensive R1 line. The changes aren’t massive—the R1 got a refresh back in 2024 that saw the R1S SUV and R1T pickup each get some comprehensive re-engineering with new powertrain options, a new electronic architecture, and new batteries.
But among them is the No. 1 most-requested feature by Rivian R1S customers, the automaker told Ars: captain’s chairs for the second row. The six-seat interior is an alternative to a middle bench, and the Rivian captain’s chair looks thoughtfully designed, with a hidden cupholder that I’m not sure I’ve seen on any other SUV before. The chairs are also spaced so it’s easy to get to the third row, or use that volume between them for skis or snowboards or surfboards.
Rivian has also changed the trims, bringing them into line with the offer structure on the recently released R2. Instead of choosing from Dual, Tri, or R1s, Rivian is now calling them Premium and Performance; Quad stays Quad. But the base price for each stays the same: The R1T still starts at $79,990 and the R1S at $83,990.

At the United States Naval Academy, even walking comes with rules.
First-year midshipmen, known as "plebes," follow regulations dictating how to walk, eat, speak, and countless other expectations as part of their transition from civilians to officers in the US Navy and the US Marine Corps.
This decorum, tied to a deep sense of duty and pride in long-held military traditions, was on full display when I visited the 338-acre waterfront campus in Annapolis, Maryland.
The grand architecture, historic rituals, and unfailingly polite greetings from uniformed service members created a palpably reverential atmosphere.
Even visitors like me are tasked with upholding certain standards, with signs that forbid jogging, biking, or walking pets in designated ceremonial areas.
I toured the United States Naval Academy in August during Plebe Parents Weekend, when plebes complete their all-consuming, seven-week basic training and reunite with loved ones before the start of the academic year.
The 90-minute public tour brings visitors inside a sports complex, the world's largest dormitory, and the Naval Academy's landmark chapel. The most memorable part of my visit, though, came after the tour was over.
Take a look inside the elite Naval Academy.
Founded in 1845, the United States Naval Academy in Annapolis, Maryland, trains future officers in the Navy and the Marine Corps.
The Naval Academy is ranked No. #1 in US News and World Report's list of Top Public Schools. Graduates of the prestigious four-year program earn a Bachelor of Science degree as well as a military rank — ensign in the Navy or second lieutenant in the Marine Corps — which are the lowest officer ranks. Most students study some form of science, technology, engineering, or mathematics, but the Naval Academy also offers degrees in English, history, and political science.
To enroll, applicants must be US citizens between the ages of 17 and 23 and be unmarried with no dependent children. They must also obtain a letter of nomination from an official source, such as a member of Congress or the vice president of the United States, and pass physical, medical, and academic examinations.
The acceptance rate is about 9%, making it a highly selective academic institution. The Class of 2030 received 16,814 applicants for a total projected class size of 1,204 midshipmen. As of 2024, the student body was around 70% male and 30% female.
Tuition is covered by the Navy. Graduates are required to serve at least five years on active duty in the Navy or Marine Corps.
The Naval Academy's 338-acre campus is surrounded by water on three sides.
The Naval Academy was established on the former site of Fort Severn, an Army post named for the Severn River on which it sits. The curriculum includes a combination of classroom instruction and hands-on experience at sea.
After passing through security at the gate, I arrived at the Armel-Leftwich Visitor Center, where public campus tours begin.
I booked the 90-minute historical walking tour through Naval Academy Tourism for $19 per adult ticket. The grounds are also open to members of the public who are US citizens, provided they show a REAL ID and go through security at the gate.
Our tour guide rang a bell to signal the start of our tour — one of many examples of how the Naval Academy functions like a ship.
At the Naval Academy, the traditional greeting is "Welcome aboard!" Maritime terminology is the norm — floors are called decks, walls are known as bulkheads, and stairs are referred to as ladders, just as they would be on Navy ships.
Students are called midshipmen, a term dating back to the English Royal Navy in the 1600s.
Our first stop outside the visitor center was a statue of Bill the Goat, the Naval Academy's mascot.
Goats have a long history on board naval ships. The chief petty officers' quarters are still referred to as "the goat locker."
In addition to a typical sports mascot character costume depicting Bill the Goat, there is also a real, live goat that gets draped in a Navy blanket for sporting events.
The title of Bill the Goat has been passed down from goat to goat; the current mascot holds the distinction of being Bill XXXVIII, or the 38th.
We continued into Lejeune Hall, which contains the USNA's Olympic-size swimming pool, Athletic Hall of Fame, and wrestling facilities.
Applicants don't need to know how to swim in order to be accepted to the Naval Academy, but by the end of their junior year, midshipmen must be able to swim 700 meters in less than 30 minutes while wearing a uniform.
Diving platforms in the aquatic center aren't only used by the diving team — midshipmen jump off of them in a graded abandon ship exercise.
Midshipmen used to be required to jump off the 10-meter platform with correct form — straight down with crossed arms and pointed toes — in order to graduate. Instead, they're now graded based on the height of the platform they jump from: 10 meters for an A, 7.5 meters for a B, and 5 meters for a C.
The Athletic Hall of Fame displays trophies and mementos from the Naval Academy's sports teams, including the annual Army vs. Navy football game.
The rivalry between the two military branches dates back generations, with the first Army-Navy football game held in 1890.
Whenever the Naval Academy's football team defeats West Point, the New York academy for training US Army officers, the game ball is spray-painted gold, inscribed with the dates of the match, and placed in a display case in Lejeune Hall.
Our tour guide made sure to point out the most recent addition from the past season, when the Navy Midshipmen defeated the Army Black Knights 17-16.
From there, we walked down Porter Road, also known as Captains Row, where department heads live while assigned to the Naval Academy.
The Naval Academy features a rotating roster of active-duty faculty members who are stationed on campus for two to four years before returning to the fleet.
The Naval Academy's Commandant of Midshipmen, who functions as the dean of students, lives in a 10,000-square-foot home on Porter Road with seven bedrooms, two-and-a-half bathrooms, and 13-foot ceilings.
In the early 1900s, architect Ernest Flagg was commissioned to renovate and expand the campus, adding French Beaux-Arts buildings such as Dahlgren Hall.
Built in 1903, Dahlgren Hall was the first building completed as part of Flagg's renovations. Built to resemble a Paris train station, it is named for Rear Adm. John A. Dahlgren, a Civil War military leader known as the "father of American naval ordnance" for founding the Navy's Ordnance Department.
Originally built as an armory, it now serves as a multipurpose space and houses the Naval Academy Business Services Division.
Dahlgren Hall has hosted sporting events, ceremonies, and dances, and it even housed an indoor ice-skating rink from 1974 to 2006.
When I visited during Plebe Parents Weekend, Dahlgren Hall hosted tables with information about student services and a place to purchase meal tickets to dine in King Hall.
A replica of a 1911 Wright Brothers B-1 plane, the first aircraft to ever fly at the Naval Academy, hung from the ceiling.
Orville Wright sent the Wright Model B-1 aircraft to what was then the Naval Academy's armory in 1911.
The plane's 60-horsepower engine was too weak to take off on its own, so pioneering naval aviator Lt. John Rodgers took flight with the help of midshipmen who tied ropes to the plane and ran.
The plane reached an altitude of 500 feet and flew for 15 minutes.
Outside Dahlgren Hall, a monument honoring the US Navy's Submarine Force pays tribute to those who "serve beneath the seas."
Commemorating the centennial of the US Submarine Force in 2000, the monument features faces engraved in the waves representing those on "eternal patrol," the traditional term for submariners lost at sea.
Bancroft Hall, which the Naval Academy describes as the largest dormitory in the world, is so big that it has its own ZIP code.
Designed by Flagg, Bancroft Hall features eight wings and houses all 4,400 midshipmen during their four years of study. During their first year at the Naval Academy, plebes are not allowed to walk through the center door.
Bancroft Hall is nicknamed "Mother B."
In addition to dormitories, Bancroft Hall also houses student services such as a uniform store, bookstore, tailor, cobbler, laundry rooms, and dental and medical facilities.
Midshipmen are considered to hold a non-combat role in the military and are paid a salary of $1,273.20 per month.
All of their expenses, including room, board, uniforms, and books, come out of their salary, and the remaining money is given as a stipend — $100 per month during Plebe Summer and $200 per month during the rest of their first year.
Each room has its own sink and shower, with communal bathrooms located in the halls.
Rooms can have between two and five midshipmen. While the rooms are single-sex, the dorms are co-ed.
In the dorms, midshipmen must store their uniforms and shoes in color order from light to dark, and their rooms are inspected for tidiness.
Tamanend Court, known as "T-Court," is named for the statue depicting a Native American chief whose figurehead is said to bring good luck to those in need of academic assistance.
The figurehead depicts Delaware Native American chief Tamanend, who signed a peace treaty with William Penn, the founder of Pennsylvania. The statue has also been referred to as Tecumseh, a Shawnee leader who was misidentified as the subject of the piece.
The original wooden bust of Tamanend served as the figurehead of the USS Delaware, which was scuttled, or intentionally sunk, during the Civil War to prevent it from being captured. The figurehead was salvaged from the wreck and displayed at the Naval Academy until the class of 1891 created a bronze version that could better withstand the elements.
Legend has it that flipping a penny into Tamanend's quiver of arrows can help midshipmen secure a passing grade, resulting in the statue's nickname of "God of the 'C.'"
Another well-known landmark on campus is the Herndon Monument, a 21-foot-tall obelisk that serves as the centerpiece of a riotous tradition.
In a ritual marking the end of their plebe status, plebes form a human pyramid to scale the monument and place a hat, known as a "dixie cup," on top. The catch: the monument is coated with grease, and the plebes are shot with water cannons as they attempt the feat.
The longest-ever Herndon climb took over four hours.
As we walked across campus, our tour guide pointed out curved walkways — shortcuts that are forbidden to plebes.
In order to train future leaders, the Naval Academy first teaches midshipmen how to follow orders without question.
Plebes follow a strict code of conduct during their first year. In addition to being barred from curved pathways on campus, plebes are required to "square their walk," meaning they must make only 90-degree turns.
Rule violations can result in disciplinary actions.
The final stop on our tour was the Naval Academy Chapel and the Crypt of John Paul Jones.
The chapel, a National Historic Landmark, was also designed by Flagg and dedicated in 1908. Its formerly green oxidized copper dome was replaced in 2020.
The chapel can seat 2,000 people.
The stained-glass windows lining the walls, which are gifts from previous classes, depict biblical references to the sea.
Pew 51 is roped off, left empty for prisoners of war and those missing in action.
The pew always features fresh flowers, and its candle is lit during services.
"Commission Invisible," a stained-glass window by Tiffany Studios, depicts a midshipman reading his commission at graduation.
There are also windows honoring naval leaders such as Adm. David Glasgow Farragut and former Naval Academy superintendent Adm. David Dixon Porter.
Beneath the worship space is the Crypt of John Paul Jones, widely regarded as America's first naval hero.
A former Royal Navy member born in Scotland in 1747, Jones joined the Continental Navy and helped defeat the British in the War of Independence. He is credited with originating the battle cry, "I have not yet begun to fight!"
My tour ended in time for me to catch the Noon Meal Formation, an eight-minute ceremony that serves as both a roll call and a display of military tradition.
In the Noon Meal Formation, held every weekday aside from Wednesdays, all 4,400 midshipmen line up outside Bancroft Hall. After the Naval Academy's six battalions declare that their members are "all present or accounted for," they march in formation into King Hall for lunch, accompanied by the United States Naval Academy Band.
The roots of the Noon Meal Formation date back to the Civil War. It has been held at the Naval Academy since 1905, serving as an exercise in accountability and leaving no one behind.
The assembled crowd, many of them family members visiting for Plebe Parents Weekend, watched in reverent silence as each battalion's presence was announced.
I was awed by how each midshipman stood absolutely still and moved in perfect synchronization.
During Plebe Parents Weekend, plebes see their families for the first time since arriving at the Naval Academy when the ceremony concludes.
During an intensive seven-week indoctrination program known as Plebe Summer, plebes undergo basic training before the academic year begins and are only allowed two timed phone calls home in that period.
Plebe Summer concludes with Plebe Parents Weekend, where family members can witness their transformation.
As soon as the plebes were dismissed, the air of formality evaporated as family members cheered and rushed to embrace their loved ones.
All around me, the precise lines and regimented formations dissolved into a swell of hugs, tears, and delighted squeals.
"I'm so proud of you!" one mother cried as her daughter sobbed in her arms. "I love you so much!"
Surrounded by so many emotional reunions, I felt myself welling up, too.
The Naval Academy's stunning architecture and rich heritage alone make it worth a trip, but the Noon Meal Formation is not to be missed.
I highly recommend booking an early tour that leaves enough time to watch the midshipmen line up and march with military precision outside Bancroft Hall at noon. It's one thing to learn about the Naval Academy's storied history. It's another to witness its legacy of high standards in action.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

Wireless charging makes a daily task just a little bit easier, and Google’s versatile Pixelsnap Charger with Stand is one of the best wireless chargers at full price. And right now, it's at a 50 percent discount, making it a bargain worth bagging.
Mirroring Google’s curvy Pixel range with a rounded form and soft-touch finish, the Pixelsnap is a regular puck-style Qi2 25W magnetic charger that usually costs $40 on its own. Right now, you can get it and the curvy stand that it pops into for just $35. Perfect if you want to prop your phone up on the nightstand and have it double as an alarm clock, for example.
If you’re not familiar, Qi2 wireless charging is like Apple’s MagSafe; it enables you to stick your phone onto a charger using a ring of magnets, ensuring perfect alignment for the most efficient and speedy wireless charging possible. I love being able to stick my phone onto the charger at night without fumbling around for a cable.
The Pixelsnap sports the very latest Qi2 25W release, so it can charge supported phones, like the Pixel 10 Pro XL, Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra, and the iPhone 17 series at up to 25 watts. The Pixelsnap can also charge older iPhones, the rest of the Pixel 10 range, and various other Samsung phones at 15 watts.
Speed might not be the most important thing for you if you charge overnight, like I do, but the Pixelsnap Charger with Stand also has a smart design that’s pretty handy when your phone is running low at the end of the day: you can pop the charger puck out, and it will stick to the back of your phone so you can continue to scroll while it charges.

How to Use AI to Prepare for a Job Interview
Before we get to the applications, which indeed make job interview preparation an easy affair, you must understand the importance of a solid foundation to begin with. Fortunately, this groundwork only requires leveraging existing AI tools you may already be using. After getting to know the details of the job interview, mainstream AI models, such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Claude, and more, can be directed to put you at an advantage from the very initial phase of your preparation. Below is what you must do first.
→ Understand the Role and Generate Role-Specific Interview Questions
Most, if not all, job descriptions are little more than a pile of technical and corporate jargon, often failing to clearly state the requirements. Misaligned interview expectations may already put you in a bad spot during the interview, so you must ensure that you are well-versed with the job description. AI models can help you do so with a few prompts, but you must include a few crucial elements to get the best results. With all this, don’t forget to upload your updated resume for a tailored response.
For starters, you cannot miss out on knowing the core competencies required for the job you’re applying for. AI can help you identify the top non-negotiable technical and soft skills that the recruiter expects of you. Such attributes are often not understood by many applicants, which prevents them from brushing up on existing skills or learning the required ones. Next, your prompt must include identifying the success metrics, or the key performance indicators of the role.
Because every hiring takes place to solve a specific problem of the organization, it’s crucial to have an idea about the performance expectations the recruiter may have from you. For tech roles, it usually revolves around solving existing issues, improving existing processes, and related tasks. In contrast, non-tech roles focus on increasing client retention, establishing business relationships, and related tasks.
Lastly, you must also ask AI to groom you based on your resume. It will help you determine whether your resume aligns well with the role and whether any specific skills need to be spotlighted. AI can not only identify potential loopholes but also help you present your projects to the interviewer in the most convincing way possible. With this initial study of the role’s requirements, you can certainly answer questions and defend yourself with confidence.
→ Study About the Company
While most candidates think they know the company they’re applying to well, the truth is, not many perform a proper deep dive. It is an important part of interview preparation, as knowing the company helps you give more relevant answers instead of generic ones.
AI makes company research much easier, but don’t simply ask it to “tell me about the company.” Start with its current market position, products, competitors, recent announcements, and anything else directly relevant to the role.
Foremost, your prompt should include information about the company’s current market position. You can assist the AI model by attaching the company’s press releases, financial reports, product launch notes, public announcements, and more. Financial reports can also be used to project the company’s future trends, map future goals, and more, which are worth knowing about.
It’s also essential to understand the company’s competitors, as it can help you frame your answers to interview questions in the company’s favor. While you are unlikely to find many, you can ask the AI model to identify and propose viable solutions to the company’s publicly available problems. It can be a significant advantage when handled appropriately and also serves as a good background for obvious questions, such as “What will you bring to the table?” and “Why should we hire you?”
→ Analyze the Interviewer
If you know who will be interviewing you, publicly available professional information can help you prepare better. Their LinkedIn profile, current role, past experience, or area of expertise may give you a fair idea of which parts of your background they are more likely to focus on.
You can provide this information to an AI model and ask it to suggest questions that someone in a similar role may ask. Don’t treat those questions as predictions, though. Use them simply to broaden your preparation and identify areas you may otherwise overlook.
This information is also useful when preparing questions to ask towards the end of the interview. Relevant questions about their team, role, or experience with the company will usually come across better than generic ones.
→ Generate Behavioral, Situational, and Technical Interview Questions
A recommended way to ensure success in an interview is to prepare for the likely questions. The question set should not only include the basic ones, but also challenging ones to put you on the spot. That way, your real-world performance will be sufficient for selection. To begin with, the basics: you can ask AI models to generate common behavioral interview questions, such as “Introduce yourself” and “Why should we hire you?” “What if we don’t select you?” “What makes you fit for this role?” and the like.
The answers to the above questions will be based on your resume and cognitive ability, which is what AI models can help you with. Next, to tackle the technical questions, your prompt must instruct the AI model to fire deep-dive technical, situational, and project-based questions at you. During all this, you can rate your technical skills and promptly improve any weak areas.
Despite the discomfort, ask the AI model to generate questions from the perspective of an interviewer who is not interested in hiring you. Understand the questions, as they can prove to be great at identifying gaps in your resume, incompetencies, and more. You can also ask the AI model to question the relevance of your past experiences, push back aggressively on your answers, and more. This will only improve your chances of getting selected.

In case you are unaware, most mainstream AI models offer voice modes that are perfect for back-and-forth questioning, making them ideal for interview practice. It’s not surprising that merely reading the questions and thinking you can answer them won’t cut it, which is why you need a simulation of the interview.
