Useful AI Prompts for Job Interview Preparation
Mainstream AI models like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude can be surprisingly effective for interview preparation if you give them enough context. A common approach among job seekers is to provide the actual job description and resume, then have the AI conduct the interview one question at a time instead of generating a generic list of questions. Here are a few prompts worth trying.
1. Analyze the Job Description and My Resume
I am preparing for an interview for the job below. Act as an experienced hiring manager and analyze both the job description and my resume.
Identify:
The five most important skills or requirements for this role
The parts of my resume that match them best
Important requirements where my experience looks weak or unclear
Questions an interviewer is likely to ask about those gaps
Technical or industry topics I should revise
Five achievements from my resume that I should make sure to highlight
Don’t invent experience or skills that aren’t present in my resume.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
2. Conduct a Realistic Mock Interview
Act as the hiring manager interviewing me for the role below. Use my resume and the job description as your primary context.
Conduct this like a real interview. Ask only one question at a time and wait for my complete answer before asking the next one. Ask natural follow-up questions based on what I actually say instead of following a fixed list.
Include a mix of behavioral, situational, resume-based, role-specific, and technical questions where relevant.
Do not give me hints or feedback while the interview is taking place. Once the interview is finished, score my performance on answer quality, relevance, clarity, confidence, and completeness. Then identify my five biggest weaknesses and tell me how to improve each one.
Job description: [paste]
Resume: [paste/upload]
3. Give Me a Difficult Mock Interview
Act as a skeptical interviewer who isn’t yet convinced that I am the right person for this role.
Use my resume and the job description to identify weak points, career gaps, vague achievements, missing skills, questionable claims, or areas where another candidate may be stronger.
Ask me one difficult question at a time. If my answer is vague, generic, evasive, or unsupported, push back and ask a follow-up question. Don’t compliment every answer or make the interview artificially easy.
At the end, tell me which answers could hurt my chances in the real interview and show me how I could make them stronger without exaggerating my experience.
4. Build My STAR Interview Stories
Help me prepare 5 reusable stories from my career for behavioral interview questions.
Use my resume and the experiences I provide to identify strong examples involving leadership, conflict, failure, problem-solving, teamwork, initiative, and working under pressure.
For each story, organize the answer using STAR:
Situation: What was happening?
Task: What was I responsible for?
Action: What specifically did I do?
Result: What changed because of my actions?
Keep Situation and Task brief and spend more time on Action and Result. Ask me for missing details rather than inventing them. Where possible, help me quantify the result.
Finally, tell me which common behavioral interview questions each story could answer.
Excel in Interviews With These AI Tools
AI has made preparing for job interviews a lot less daunting than it used to be. For most people, mainstream AI models such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude are already good enough for understanding a job description, researching a company, preparing likely questions, and improving answers.
Dedicated AI interview tools become useful when you want something closer to the real thing. Exponent Practice and Interviewing.io make more sense for technical candidates, Yoodli is particularly good for communication and behavioral practice, while MyInterviewAI works well for resume-based preparation. Big Interview helps with overall delivery, Huru AI makes quick job-specific practice easy, and Ophy AI covers the widest range of interview-preparation needs.
Whichever tool you choose, don’t stop after one mock interview. Upload your latest resume and the actual job description, complete a practice session, review where you struggled, and repeat it after fixing those areas. Two or three focused mock interviews will be far more useful than memorizing dozens of AI-generated answers.
Critique My Interview Answer
I will give you an interview question followed by my answer.
Evaluate the answer as a demanding hiring manager. First, tell me:
Whether I actually answered the question
What was convincing
What sounded vague or generic
Whether I gave enough evidence
Whether I spent too much time on irrelevant context
What follow-up question an interviewer would probably ask
If it is a behavioral question, also evaluate it using the STAR method.
Only after giving me this critique, provide a stronger version that retains my real experience and sounds natural when spoken aloud. Don’t turn it into a polished corporate script that nobody would actually say in an interview.
FAQs about AI Interview Tools
Can ChatGPT help me prepare for a job interview?
Yes. You can give ChatGPT your resume and job description and ask it to identify likely interview questions, evaluate your answers, conduct mock interviews, research the role, and point out gaps in your preparation. Voice mode makes the mock interview experience significantly more natural.
Are AI mock interviews actually useful?
They can be, especially when the AI asks follow-up questions and gives detailed feedback instead of simply generating a list of questions. They are particularly useful for repeated practice, although they shouldn't completely replace practice with another person when that is available.
Which AI interview tools are free?
Exponent Practice offers a limited number of free peer mock interviews, while Yoodli has a free tier. Huru AI provides free access to try its mock interviews, and Ophy AI offers free starting credits. The exact limits can change, so check each service before signing up.
What is the best AI interview tool for software engineers?
Interviewing.io and Exponent Practice are the strongest options on this list for software engineers. They focus much more heavily on coding, system design, algorithms, and other technical interview formats than general-purpose interview coaching tools.
Can I use AI during an actual job interview?
That depends entirely on the employer and interview rules. Some companies prohibit outside assistance during interviews and assessments. Unless the interviewer explicitly allows it, the safer approach is to use AI extensively during preparation and answer the actual interview questions yourself.
How many AI mock interviews should I practice?
There is no fixed number. Instead of repeating mock interviews endlessly, complete one, review the feedback, fix the weak areas, and try again. A few focused sessions with clear improvement between them are more useful than doing many interviews without reviewing your mistakes.

Nihang in 60s, worked as 'sewadar': What we know about Sukhbir Singh Badal's attacker
Sukhbir Singh Badal was attacked while he was walking towards the langar hall after paying obeisance at the gurdwara.
Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) president Sukhbir Singh Badal was attacked with a kirpan by a Nihang at Gurdwara Mata Sahib Kaur on the outskirts of Nanded Sahib in Maharashtra on Thursday.
Badal suffered an injury to his right hand and was shifted to a nearby hospital. He is now out of danger, HT has learnt.
READ ALSO | Ex-Punjab deputy CM Sukhbir Singh Badal attacked with 'kirpan' outside gurdwara in Maharashtra's Nanded
Who attacked Sukhbir Singh Badal?
The attacker was a Nihang dressed in blue attire and is reportedly in his mid-sixties. His identity has not yet been revealed. Security personnel accompanying Badal overpowered him and handed him over to the local police for questioning.
According to Jaimal Singh Dhillon, a functionary at Takht Nanded Sahib, the gurdwara is under the control of a Nihang Samparday and the attacker is said to be from Punjab.
The historic Nanded gurdwara is managed by a splinter group of Shiromani Panth Akali Budha Dal 96 Crori, a major Nihang organisation headed by Baba Maan Singh. The local jathedar is Baba Teja Singh. The accused Nihang was reportedly serving as a sewadar at the gurdwara.
Where was Sukhbir Singh Badal attacked?
The attack took place at Gurdwara Mata Sahib Kaur on the outskirts of Nanded, around 15 km from Takht Nanded Sahib, one of the five temporal seats of the Sikhs.
Badal was attacked while he was walking towards the langar hall after paying obeisance at the gurdwara. The shrine is controlled by a Nihang sect and is not managed by the board that oversees the main Nanded Sahib Gurdwara.
Maharashtra chief minister Devendra Fadnavis sought details of the incident from the Nanded Superintendent of Police and directed authorities to investigate the motive behind the attack.
‘Attack on Punjab’s unity’: SAD leader
SAD national vice-president Sanjeev Talwar called the attack on party chief Badal a serious security lapse.
“Sukhbir Singh Badal is a promoter of Hindu-Sikh unity, he speaks of Punjab and Punabiyat,” Talwar said. “This is not a direct attack on Sukhbir Singh Badal but an attack on the unity and integrity of Punjab,” he added.
“Such attack on someone who has Z+ security and is a former Deputy CM will certainly be considered a security lapse,” he said.
Why was Sukhbir Badal in Nanded?
Badal reached Nanded on Wednesday with his family and a group of close associates for a three-day visit. He organised an Akhand Path at the gurdwara.
Earlier on Thursday, Badal was offered a siropa by the head priests at Sachkhand Nanded Sahib, the main gurdwara in Nanded and one of the five temporal seats of the Sikhs. Bathinda MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal and other family members were also present.
Gurdwara Mata Sahib Kaur is located around 15 km from the main Nanded Sahib gurdwara and is under the control of a Nihang Samparday.
Badal’s second attack in less than two years
The Nanded incident is the second attack on Sukhbir Badal in less than two years. On December 4, 2024, former militant Narain Singh Chaura allegedly attempted to assassinate Badal at the entrance of the Golden Temple in Amritsar.
Chaura fired at the SAD chief from close range, but the bullet narrowly missed after a security officer grabbed his pistol. The bullet struck the shrine wall.
No one was injured in that incident. Chaura was overpowered and arrested.

New Delhi: The government aims to make policymaking more responsive by using people’s experiences, grievances, and suggestions to identify gaps in public services and turn concerns into broader policy and reforms, said two people aware of the matter.
It is the first time that the government is introducing such a mechanism, they said.
The finance ministry, as the nodal agency, has asked ministries and departments to examine their grievance and complaint mechanisms and shortlist five complaints or suggestions that could potentially be converted into policy changes.
Reform Utsav was christened in June to mark 12 years of the government.
To be sure, under existing practice, departments act on complaints and seek to resolve them within the stipulated timeframe. Under the new approach, however, complaints and grievances will also be screened from a policy perspective. Officials handling consumer grievance portals will analyse the complaints and identify those that could translate into policy suggestions or reforms. The contribution of the complainant or end user will also be acknowledged as an input to the policy reform process.
The initiative marks a shift in the way citizen grievances are viewed. Instead of treating complaints only as individual cases to be resolved, ministries have been asked to identify recurring concerns that may indicate gaps in the underlying rules, procedures, or the scheme's implementation. The thinking is that citizens who use government schemes and services are often best placed to identify problems at the last mile.
Bigger role for citizen’s voice
The ministries will send the shortlisted suggestions to the nodal ministry, where they will be reviewed by an inter-ministerial group to be constituted for the purpose. Any policy or procedural changes will be approved by the competent authority in accordance with the existing rules.
“The key objective is to make policy corrections based on inputs from end users who experience gaps in the delivery of schemes and services on a regular basis. We are scanning the complaints and filtering those that can help bring about reforms, particularly in public-centric welfare schemes,” said the first among the two persons cited above.
“The intent is to increase the participation of citizens at every stage of policy formulation and recognise their suggestions as an important input for policymaking,” this person said, adding that the aim is to make reforms more of the people, by the people and for the people.
Citizens can file complaints through several government channels—Centralised Public Grievance Redress and Monitoring System (CPGRAMS), the National Consumer Helpline, the PMO grievance mechanism, ministry portals, and dedicated helplines. Ministries are now mining this feedback pool to spot recurring issues and shape policy reforms.
The complaints or grievances could span a wide range of sectors, including banking services, manufacturing, production-linked incentive (PLI) schemes, agriculture, consumer affairs, food distribution, petroleum products, road transport and several others.
Stronger people's participation
“The exercise also seeks to give a stronger Jan Bhagidari, or people’s participation, dimension to the government’s reform agenda. Rather than relying only on internal administrative reviews or fresh consultation exercises, ministries would draw reform ideas from feedback that citizens have already provided while accessing government services,” the second person said.
Queries sent to spokespersons of the PMO and all ministries, including finance, Department of Personnel and Training (DoPT), consumer affairs, education, labour and employment, remained unanswered till press time.
“When there are flaws in the basic structure of a policy, cosmetic changes will not be enough. Complaints and suggestions from citizens are important because they reflect the concerns and gaps people experience on the ground. Issues such as inadequate investment in research and development, rising corruption or weaknesses in implementation cannot be addressed merely by making incremental changes. The government needs to identify the root causes and undertake meaningful policy corrections,” said Arun Kumar, noted economist and retired professor of Jawaharlal Nehru University.

Bangladesh dominate Australia despite Smith reprieve
- Published
First Test, Darwin (day one of five)
Australia 198: Smith 71; Mahmud 6-55
Bangladesh 96-1: Mominul 35*, Tanzid 32*
Bangladesh trail by 102 runs
Bangladesh dominated Australia on day one of the first Test, despite Steve Smith benefitting from being given not out on review to a ball he later said he nicked.
Smith was on seven when the Tigers appealed for caught behind off Ebadot Hossain, but umpire Kumar Dharmasena was unmoved.
The tourists reviewed the decision and Smith appeared to start to walk off, only for the Snicko technology to show a flat line as the ball passed the bat and so the not out decision stood.
Smith went on to make 71 but his team-mates otherwise struggled in Darwin as Tigers fast bowler Hasan Mahmud took a career-best 6-55 to help dismiss the hosts for 198.
Bangladesh reached 96-1 at the close, trailing by 102 runs.

When asked if he thought he had edged the ball, Smith said: "I think so, yeah. I was lucky? Yeah, it seems that way. You got to take it sometimes.

Snicko was the source of several controversies during the last Ashes series in Australia - host wicketkeeper Alex Carey was given a reprieve after a mistake by the operator of the technology, while England wicketkeeper Jamie Smith was twice involved in contentious decisions.

Congo’s Ebola outbreak has spread to a sixth province, raising fresh concerns over the rapid pace of transmission and the ability of health authorities to contain the disease.
A death was reported in Bas-Uele province, which had not previously recorded cases in the current outbreak, Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya said on Thursday (August 13). The man had travelled from Isiro in neighbouring Haut-Uele province to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died.
The development comes as the World Health Organization warns that the outbreak in eastern Congo could become the deadliest Ebola epidemic in history.
More than 4,500 cases and 2,100 deaths have been reported, according to the latest government figures cited in the source material.
The WHO has described the outbreak as the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak yet and said it is on track to surpass the previous deadliest outbreak, which killed more than 11,000 people during the 2014-16 epidemic in West Africa.
The current death toll has been reached almost three times faster than during that earlier outbreak, highlighting the speed at which the virus is spreading.
Six of Congo’s 26 provinces have now been affected.
The outbreak was initially concentrated in eastern Congo, but the latest death in Bas-Uele marks the spread into a sixth province.
The man who died in Buta had travelled from Isiro in Haut-Uele, raising concerns about transmission between provinces.
Health authorities say between 60% and 70% of new cases are being detected outside the network of monitored contacts. This makes it harder for health workers to identify chains of transmission and isolate people who may have been exposed.
The WHO has described the spread as “alarming”.
Health authorities are confronting several challenges at the same time.
Some healthcare workers have gone on strike because they have not been paid. In Ituri province, workers at the Nizi Treatment Center stopped work on Thursday, temporarily closing the facility after saying they had not received salaries for three months.
The outbreak is also unfolding amid threats from rebel groups, public anger and misinformation, including claims that Ebola does not exist.
These conditions can make it harder for health workers to reach communities, identify patients and persuade people to cooperate with disease-control measures.
Congo officially declared the outbreak on May 15. However, the WHO later said genetic sequencing showed that the outbreak had actually begun months earlier, in February.
That finding suggests the virus had been circulating before authorities formally recognised the outbreak.
The delay also illustrates why health officials are concerned about the true scale of the epidemic.
The current outbreak is being caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare species of Ebola virus.
Unlike some other Ebola outbreaks, there are no approved vaccines or treatments specifically for the Bundibugyo virus, according to the information provided.
Ebola is highly contagious through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, including blood, vomit and semen. Transmission can also occur through contaminated materials and surfaces such as clothing and bedding.
The disease can cause severe illness and can be fatal.
There is some progress on potential treatments.
Clinical trials of two possible treatments for this type of Ebola began last month in Ituri province, which has been among the worst-affected areas.
However, the outbreak continues to spread while researchers and health authorities work to determine how effective these treatments are.
The biggest concern is that the virus appears to be moving faster than the response.
Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, WHO regional director for Africa, summed up the challenge by saying: “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us.”
The spread into Bas-Uele, the high proportion of cases occurring outside monitored contacts and disruptions at treatment facilities could make containment more difficult.
With more than 2,100 deaths already reported and the outbreak affecting six provinces, health authorities face a race to identify infections, trace contacts and prevent further transmission before the epidemic grows even larger.

I've flown United Airlines across the Atlantic at least a dozen times for my job, and it's always been hit-or-miss.
Much of that comes down to the aircraft type: Some of United's older planes, like its Boeing long-haul 767s and 777s, still have dated cabins and older technology.
But amid booming premium demand, United is working to modernize its fleet and cabin experience from nose to tail, including its aging Boeing 777-200s, which have an average age of about 27 years.
I flew on one of the renovated 777 planes from Newark, New Jersey, to London in July to experience the upgrades. My specific plane was first delivered in 1997, but the modern seats and large seatback screens with Bluetooth connectivity made that hard to tell.
I was also impressed by the meals. United's food has often left much to be desired on my previous long-haul flights, but the chicken dish and breakfast pastry I had on this trip were surprisingly flavorful.
Here's what the full seven-hour basic economy flight was like. Business Insider paid $900 for the round-trip ticket.
My basic economy ticket came with a carry-on, a personal item, and a seat in the back.
Unlike its domestic basic economy fares, which include only a personal item, United's long-haul discount fares also permit a free carry-on.
The ticket allowed me to select a seat at check-in, and the only remaining aisle seat — my preferred seat — was in the center section of the very last row. It was near the galley but ended up being a great place to escape the crowded coach cabin.
I used my United credit card to get a bunch of free perks.
I have the United Explorer credit card, meaning I get a free checked bag, two free United Club lounge passes a year, and Group 2 boarding.
I used all of the perks during this flight. I lightened my haul by checking my duffle, and I was among the first to board the jet. And the United Club was huge; I enjoyed a light dinner and drinks before my red-eye flight.
The seat was comfortable with standard legroom, but the cabin was dense.
United's renovated 777 has comfortable economy seats, complete with a headrest, a large seatback screen, power ports, and Bluetooth.
However, these planes have a 3x4x3 seat layout. That means it's a 10-abreast cabin with 17-inch-wide seats, which are an inch narrower than the setup before United changed it in the mid 2010s.
Having flown on 777s with both layouts in the past and being average-sized, I couldn't tell the difference.
But I can imagine the middle seats in the middle section may feel cramped, so it may be worth paying extra for an aisle or window seat.
I liked the privacy of the last row.
I didn't pre-select a seat like I usually do to secure an aisle, planning to pay if I couldn't snag one for free at check-in. Luckily, there was one left in the very last row of the cabin: seat 53D.
While many people avoid proximity to the galleries and lavatories, I don't mind the easy access to the bathrooms and the extra privacy, since I'm out of immediate view of everyone else.
The seatback screen had Bluetooth and plenty of entertainment options.
I was impressed with the Bluetooth connectivity. United has been rolling out the feature on its planes for years and plans to equip over 800 planes with the perk by 2032. But the rollout has been slower for its widebodies, so it was a nice surprise to find it on the old 777 I flew.
The setup was easy: I put the headphones into pairing mode and disconnected them from other devices. I prefer using my own headset over United's cheap wired ones, which I find make the audio scratchy and too quiet.
The food was better than I remembered.
I've not always found United's long-haul food to be the best, but it has actively been addressing the problem. It recently partnered with professional chefs to curate a new menu for its Polaris business-class passengers, and I can tell it has beefed up its economy offerings, too.
My economy meal service was much better than I remembered from previous flights. We got cheese and crackers shortly after takeoff, and then dinner a little later.
I had the chicken dish with a side salad, bread, and a brownie. There was also a beef and a vegetarian option; my friend had the beef and liked it.
Breakfast was a turkey ham and cheese sandwich. Everything tasted great, and I liked the pacing of the meals.
United provided a blanket and a pillow.
A blanket and pillow are standard on long-haul flights, especially red-eyes. The blanket was soft and warm, and the pillow had a cutout so I could wear it around my neck.
Pairing that with the headrest made sleep somewhat easier, though I struggle to sleep on planes anyway. I slept about four hours total.
I'm happy United is investing in more than just business class.
I've always considered United a good airline, despite its sometimes lackluster food, but its modern cabin and improved meals made a noticeable difference on my economy flight to London.
And although not on my plane just yet, I'm excited to see United's new "Relax Row" — essentially a bed in economy — will be added to its Boeing 777 and 787 widebodies starting next year.
United has also added a snack bar and extra elbow-room seats in economy on its brand-new Airbus A321XLR jets.
It's refreshing to see an airline investing in the economy cabin, where a majority of its customers sit, rather than just its VIP sections.

Russia is increasingly using drones with jet engines in attacks against Ukraine, forcing its air defenders to grapple with the challenge of high-speed threats that are more difficult to intercept.
Col. Yurii Ihnat, the spokesperson for the Ukrainian Air Force, revealed in remarks shared with Business Insider on Thursday that "jet-powered drones account for as much as two-thirds of all drones used" in some Russian attacks.
Ihnat's assessment appears to be the highest publicly disclosed estimate yet of the share of jet-powered drones in Russian bombardments.
Earlier estimates provided in recent months put that figure at up to 20%, already a sharp increase from last year, when jet-powered drones were reported only rarely.
In early June, Gen. Oleksandr Syrskyi, Ukraine's former commander in chief, said that Russia planned to increase the proportion of jet-powered drones to 50%. "This presents us with new challenges that require a timely response," he warned at the time.
Russia has routinely used a strike drone called the Geran-2 to attack Ukraine. This propeller-driven aircraft, modeled after the Iranian Shahed-136, is packed with explosives and can fly at roughly 115 mph.
Russia has developed a few faster variants of the Geran attack drone that are powered by mini turbojet engines. The Geran-3 can cruise at speeds of over 200 mph, while the Geran-4 can reach 310 mph. The newest model, the Geran-5, can fly at speeds up to around 375 mph. It lacks the delta-wing shape and more closely resembles a cruise missile's profile.
The jet-powered drones carry explosive payloads for hundreds of miles before striking a target in Ukraine.
Yehor Cherniev, the deputy chairman of the Ukrainian parliament's national security, defense, and intelligence committee, told Business Insider that Ukraine has managed to intercept more than 90% of Russian cruise missiles and Geran-2 drones.
He said that Russia has decided to rely more on its jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles, far more challenging threats.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Thursday that a Russian jet-powered drone struck a passenger train in the southern Odesa region, killing at least two people in the latest attack.
Russia has been expanding the infrastructure at its air bases to support the launch of jet-powered drones, which take off on long rails and accelerate to flight speed before the engine takes over.
Ukraine's GUR military intelligence agency said in May that Russia was ramping up the employment of jet-powered drones in response to the effectiveness of Ukrainian interceptor drones, while also improving their design to make them more maneuverable.
The interceptor drones, which are cheap and destroy their targets by colliding with them or exploding nearby, were initially made to counter the slower Geran-2s.
However, Ukrainian defense companies are developing a new class of faster interceptor drones to keep pace with the high-speed jet-powered Gerans, which are harder for Kyiv to shoot down.
Ukrainian firm Skyfall told Business Insider that its new interceptor, the P1-Sun JetKiller, had already downed more than a dozen jet-powered threats by late July. The company said it planned to begin mass production this month, with other developers pursuing similar timelines.
Beyond the interceptors, Ukrainian forces also have mobile air defense units, electronic warfare systems, fighter jets, and missiles to engage Russian drones.
The uptick in Russian jet-powered drones comes as Ukraine struggles with worsening ballistic missile attacks and depleted stockpiles of Western-made interceptors.

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Sri Lanka’s southern coastal city stirred awake to the insistent whisper of rains at dawn. Water slanted down like sharp threads but once the clouds dissipated, the heat slithered in like a shroud that choked. As Thursday wore on, Shubman Gill’s men trained hard at the Galle International Stadium.
After the net session, India’s bowling coach Morne Morkel jogged a bit, and then faced the media. In the lead-up to the first Test against Sri Lanka from Saturday, questions ranged from team-composition to pitch-analysis.
India played a lone Test, the winning one against Afghanistan, earlier this year. Aware of this shortfall in cricket’s longest format, Morkel said: “We came 10 days earlier to give the guys the best opportunity to prepare. We haven’t played a lot of red-ball cricket and going back into that will be a challenge. We are quite excited to see how these guys can stand up and create pressure.”
On a surface expected to aid spin, Morkel did not deny the possibility of having three left-arm spinners ranging from the conventional Ravindra Jadeja and Manav Suthar to the unconventional Kuldeep Yadav, plying his chinaman wares. “Kuldeep is an attacking bowler, and with his experience and class we can’t look past. All three are different. One turns a bit more, and one is slightly more accurate. They have got the skill to get 20 wickets for us,” Morkel said.
The former South African speedster was not perturbed by the lack of experience in his pace attack: “All these guys have come a long way. Prasidh (Krishna) and (Mohammed) Siraj have played a lot of cricket back home, where it’s also tough bowling conditions. The biggest challenge will be the heat, the humidity, and the Kookaburra ball once it gets a little bit soft.”
Queried about the pitch, Morkel said: “It looks like a good surface and as the Test goes on, something will happen. We have prepared for all that can come our way. It’s more about the mental challenge now, facing these conditions, batting time, bowling those spells and getting the ball in the right areas.”
Reverse-swing was not ruled out too as Morkel explained: “It is definitely going to play a role. This morning we had quite a big shower, that will make the outfield a little softer and then it would take a bit longer for the ball to reverse. If you are a fast bowler, you will bowl short spells and you always will have an opportunity.”
Morkel was clear about the ideal strategy and it centred around excelling in the first innings and exerting pressure: “The first two days will belong to the batting side. Whatever happens at the toss, if you bat first make sure you go big and if you bowl first get the ball in the right areas.” Soon Morkel jogged away while the sun bathed the nearby Dutch fort and the Indian Ocean shimmered.

Meta is launching an optional Scam Alert feature on WhatsApp that uses on-device machine learning to flag suspicious messages. Earlier this year, Meta also launched scam detection for device linking requests on WhatsApp. The new Scam Alert feature, which is rolling out in a limited beta, shows users a warning if a chat seems like a scam:
Meta adds AI screening to detect WhatsApp scams
An AI model on your phone can try to determine if you’re getting scammed.
If the model identifies a message as a likely scam attempt, the user sees a warning in the chat, which is not visible to the other person. From there, the user can decide what to do: block, report, or continue the conversation. If they decide that a warning is incorrectly flagged, the user can mark the chat as trusted, in which case the warning is removed and Scam Alert will not flag that chat again. If a user marks that they trust a chat, they can also opt in to share the last 5 messages received with WhatsApp to help improve the feature’s accuracy.
With more than 3 billion users, WhatsApp is among the largest areas of scam activity, like wire transfers and pig butchering scams. The FTC said victims reported losing $425 million to scams via WhatsApp alone, out of more than $2.1 billion lost to social media scams in 2025.
Meta says “no message content leaves the user device for classification” when its scam detection feature is turned on and nothing is “auto-reported to WhatsApp, Meta, or anyone else.” Users can also turn off Scam Alert at any time.

The petition, filed through advocate Subhash Chandran KR, claims that since the commencement of the sit-in at Jantar Mantar on June 20, thousands of protesters, journalists and ordinary citizens have been subjected to “continuous and pervasive biometric surveillance”.
Rahim has sought a declaration that indiscriminate deployment of facial recognition and biometric surveillance against peaceful protesters is unconstitutional. He has also sought directions restraining the Delhi Police from deploying such technologies until Parliament enacts a law specifically authorising their use.
Also read: Police identify 2,873 protesters with ‘criminal backgrounds’
Petitioner seeks deletion of protesters’ biometric data
Among other reliefs, the petition seeks disclosure of the surveillance technologies, databases, standard operating procedures and vendor agreements used during the Jantar Mantar protest; deletion of protesters’ biometric data from NAFIS, CCTNS and allied databases; and a mechanism enabling individuals to ascertain whether their biometric information was collected and seek its deletion.
It has also sought directions to private vendors to permanently delete biometric information collected during the protest and certify such destruction, besides restraining them from using the data to train, develop or improve facial recognition or artificial intelligence systems.
According to the plea, the surveillance was carried out through CCTV cameras, drones, a Mobile Command and Control Vehicle and handheld devices, besides real-time facial recognition using the “Ikshana” surveillance vehicle and “AjnaLens” smart glasses. It also alleges collection of fingerprints through the NCRB’s “Abhigyan” application and their matching against the National Automated Fingerprint Identification System (NAFIS).
Plea questions legal basis for facial recognition at protests
The plea contends that there is no law authorising the biometric surveillance of people participating in a lawful protest. It argues that neither Delhi Police standing orders governing protests nor the Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022 permit such surveillance of peaceful demonstrators.
The petition relies on RTI responses obtained from the Delhi Police to claim that no privacy impact assessment was conducted before the surveillance was undertaken. It further alleges that an 80% similarity score is treated as a positive facial recognition match, despite the absence of any publicly available validation of the threshold.
It also claims that Delhi Police’s stated use of facial recognition technology is limited to tracing missing persons and identifying deceased persons, rather than policing peaceful assemblies.
Petition invokes privacy, free speech and assembly rights
The petitioner has invoked the Supreme Court’s 2017 privacy judgment in the KS Puttaswamy case, arguing that the alleged surveillance fails the constitutional requirements of legality, legitimate aim and proportionality. It contends that the indiscriminate deployment of facial recognition creates a chilling effect on the exercise of the rights to free speech and peaceful assembly under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b), apart from being arbitrary and disproportionate under Article 14.
The plea also raises concerns over the retention and possible integration of the biometric information with national criminal databases, alleging that the data could be retained indefinitely without adequate statutory safeguards, purpose limitation or a defined retention policy.

Two private companies have also been made respondents to the PIL, Aditya Infotech Ltd, which allegedly supplied the “Ikshana” facial recognition vehicle, and Dimension NXG Pvt Ltd, which allegedly supplied the AjnaLens smart glasses. The plea alleges that the companies participated in the policing exercise and may continue to possess footage, facial templates and other biometric information of protesters. It also questions whether any data-processing or data-sharing agreements, or other contractual safeguards governing access to such sensitive information, were put in place.

Vladimir Putin's first visit to disputed Pacific islands draws Tokyo protest
MOSCOW — Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday made his first visit to the Kuril Islands, a Moscow-controlled Pacific archipelago that also is claimed by Japan, which voiced a diplomatic protest over the trip.
Putin visited a fish plant, a hospital and a school on Iturup, one of the volcanic chain's southern islands. He also briefly spoke to local residents and met with the governor of Russia's Sakhalin region, Valery Limarenko.
Japan asserts territorial rights to the four southernmost islands of the chain, which it calls the Northern Territories. The Soviet Union took them from Japan in the final days of World War II, and the dispute kept the countries from signing a peace treaty formally ending their hostilities.
Decades of diplomatic efforts to negotiate a settlement haven't produced any visible results. Moscow over the years has also bolstered its military presence on the Kurils in moves that appeared to underscore its firm stance in the dispute.
Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said his country "strongly protests" Putin's visit to Iturup, which Japan calls Etorofu.
"The Northern Territories, including Etorofu (Iturup) Island, are Japan's inherent territory both historically and from the perspective of international law," Motegi said in a statement.
He summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to the ministry in Tokyo and lodged a strong protest over the visit, requesting that he "promptly report the message back to Moscow," the minister told reporters afterward.
Later Thursday, the Russian Embassy in Japan called Tokyo's protest "unfounded" and said Nozdrev had explained that "the southern Kuril Islands are an integral part of the Russian Federation and became part of it following World War II on legitimate international grounds."
Putin's travels are "sovereign decisions of the Russian leadership and can't be subject to discussion with foreign states," the statement added.
Japan also protested in 2021 when Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin visited Iturup.
Putin in recent days has visited several regions in Siberia and the Far East. Before coming to Iturup, he stopped on Sakhalin Island to attend the final part of drills by Russia's Pacific Fleet.
Speaking aboard a warship that was participating in the naval exercises, Putin said Wednesday that the current status of the Kuril Islands "is enshrined in international documents as a reality that arose following the outcome of World War II."
"But even here, Russia was prepared to seek a solution with the goal of concluding a peace treaty with Japan," he said.
Putin said that in the past, Moscow "had developed constructive relations with a number of Japanese leaders, including the tragically deceased former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe, who did much to bring Japan and Russia closer together, to align our positions."
Japan imposed sanctions on Russia after it sent troops into Ukraine in February 2022 and "listed Russia as a source of primary threats," a change in that constructive relationship, he added.
Russia remains ready "to cooperate with all its neighbors, including Japan and other states in the region," Putin said.
Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Putin's visit is "incompatible with the Japanese position on the Northern Territories" and is "absolutely unacceptable."
She said the visit was a further blow to the already-strained ties between the two countries over Ukraine, and that Moscow should understand the consequences.
"We must say this visit has further hardened Japanese public sentiment toward Russia and has made it more difficult to restore bilateral relations in the medium to long term," she said. "We hope the Russian side fully understands the seriousness of this."
One of the reasons Japan has made the effort to maintain ties with Russia is to allow former Japanese residents to return to the islands and pay tribute at their graves as a humanitarian consideration.
Dmitry Medvedev, Russia's former president and prime minister who now serves as deputy chair of the country's Security Council, responded to Takaichi's remarks on X by saying, "This chatter won't change a thing."
The Kuril Islands "were, are, and will remain Russian land," Medvedev, who himself visited the Kuril Islands four times as president and prime minister, wrote. "Anyone who fails to understand this will face the monstrous consequences of their delusion."

Jharkhand student protests began on 25 July 2026 over alleged irregularities in the 14th JPSC Preliminary and JSSC-CGL examinations, including allegations of OMR tampering. Led by student leader Devendra Nath Mahto, protesters have demanded cancellation of the exams and an independent CBI probe. On 10 August 2026, thousands of students marched towards the Jharkhand Assembly, where police used lathi charges and water cannons. The government has since agreed to cancel three JPSC examinations, but students continue to demand a CBI probe into the alleged irregularities. As of 13 August 2026, the protests have entered their 20th day, with Mahto continuing his hunger strike and political support for the movement growing (here, here, here, and here).
Amid this, a video is being shared on social media (here, here, and here) with the claim that it shows Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) workers pelting stones during the Jharkhand student protest in an attempt to defame the ongoing movement. Let’s verify the claim made in the post in this article.
Claim: The video shows BJP workers pelting stones during the Jharkhand student protest in an attempt to defame the ongoing movement.
Fact: The video is unrelated to the ongoing Jharkhand student protests. It actually shows a clash between BJP and Congress workers outside the Congress office in Indore, Madhya Pradesh, on 21 February 2026, during which both sides reportedly engaged in stone-pelting. Hence, the claim made in the post is Misleading.
A reverse image search of keyframes from the viral video led us to a news report published on TheSootr’s YouTube channel on 22 February 2026 that featured the same visuals. According to the report, the video is from Indore, Madhya Pradesh, where BJP and Congress workers clashed outside the Congress office on 21 February 2026, with stone-pelting reported from both sides. This confirms that the viral video predates the Jharkhand student protests and is unrelated to the ongoing movement.
We found multiple other reports (here, and here) covering the incident. According to these reports, the BJP had announced plans to surround Congress offices in several cities in response to the controversial ‘shirtless’ protest by Youth Congress workers during the India AI Impact Summit at Bharat Mandapam in Delhi. On 21 February 2026, the situation in Indore escalated when BJP youth workers arrived to surround the Congress office and confronted Congress workers who were already present. Heated sloganeering between the two sides soon escalated into a clash, with stones, tomatoes and water bottles thrown from both sides. A sub-inspector and several media personnel were injured, and police used water cannons to disperse the protesters. Police later registered counter FIRs based on complaints from both sides at Pandharinath police station and began an investigation using CCTV footage.
We geolocated the exact place where the clash took place near the Congress party office in Indore and identified that the viral video was recorded near 2 Indore-Khandwa Road, Indore, Madhya Pradesh. A signboard for “Mica Planet” visible in the background of the video matches the location seen on Google Maps Street View. The comparison can be seen below.
To sum up, an old video of a BJP-Congress clash in Indore is shared as BJP workers pelting stones during the Jharkhand student protest.

Geneva 17 October 2024 – This afternoon, His Excellency Mr Jérôme Bonnafont, Permanent Representative of France to the United Nations in Geneva, and WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus met in the WHO headquarters for the signing of seven contribution agreements.
The contribution totalling €24 million comes through the Ministry of Europe & Foreign Affairs. It fits in the France–WHO Framework Agreement for 2020 to 2025, which provides both a strategic framework for engagement, aligned with WHO priorities, while providing legal, administrative and financial instruments for operationalizing collaboration.
This latest contribution includes a generous €4.5 million in fully flexible voluntary funds for the Core Voluntary Contributions Account (CVCA).
Additionally, France will support key areas of WHO’s work, addressing some of the most pressing health challenges, including non-communicable diseases (NCDs), urban health labs, One Health, funding for the WHO Contingency Fund for Emergencies (CFE), and several emergencies, such as the WHO response in Gaza, response to cholera outbreaks and mental health support in Ukraine.
France will also continue to support the WHO emergencies centre in Lyon which is playing a crucial role in preparedness and response to epidemics.
Ambassador Jérôme Bonnafont underscored the importance of this collaboration: “France remains deeply committed to supporting the World Health Organization in its efforts to tackle critical global health challenges. These agreements reflect our shared priorities of promoting health equity, responding to emergencies, and strengthening healthcare systems worldwide.”
Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Director-General of WHO, expressed his gratitude, stating, “We are immensely grateful to the French Government for its steadfast support to WHO, continued partnership and leadership in global health. This contribution will enable us to address key health threats, from non-communicable diseases to emergency response, helping to save lives and protect the most vulnerable populations.”
France is a strong supporter of a fully and flexibly financed WHO, providing leadership and support to the increase of assessed contributions to the Organization. France is also one of the co-hosts to WHO’s first Investment Round towards the mobilization of predictable and flexible resources for WHO’s core work on the Fourteenth General Programme of Work (2025–2028), approved by the World Health Assembly in 2024.
This signing ceremony marks another milestone in the strong and longstanding partnership between WHO and France, reinforcing their joint commitment to a healthier, safer world.

India has withdrawn from the inaugural FIFA ASEAN Cup, opting to prioritise its high-profile international friendly against five-time world champion Brazil in October, All India Football Federation (AIFF) deputy secretary general M Satyanarayanan said on Thursday.
India’s withdrawal from the upcoming tournament also means it will miss the opportunity to face some of Southeast Asia’s leading sides in a FIFA-sanctioned competition.
“We have pulled out of the FIFA ASEAN Cup since we can’t play both Brazil and FIFA ASEAN Cup,” Satyanarayanan told PTI.
ALSO READ |Spanish Super Cup to be held in Turkey in 2027
The inaugural tournament was conceived as a new international competition for teams from the ASEAN region, with India invited as one of the non-ASEAN participants.
India had initially accepted FIFA’s invitation to participate in the new tournament and was subsequently drawn in Division 1 Group A alongside Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore. The competition is scheduled to be played during the September 21-October 6 FIFA international window.
However, India’s commitment to play Brazil on October 3 at Kolkata’s Salt Lake Stadium created a scheduling clash.
The AIFF had earlier explored the possibility of fielding a separate or developmental squad in the ASEAN Cup, but has now opted to withdraw altogether and use the international window for friendlies.
The match against Brazil was officially announced last month.
Meanwhile, reports on Thursday suggested that India is exploring friendlies against teams that featured at the 2026 FIFA World Cup, with Cabo Verde and Iran among the sides being discussed. However, those fixtures have not yet been officially confirmed by the AIFF.
The AIFF’s decision marks a significant change from its plans earlier this year, when it had accepted FIFA’s invitation and signed the participation agreement.
India, who failed to qualify for the 2027 AFC Asian Cup, has struggled to secure regular high-quality opposition in recent years.

Caution: Spoilers for "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" ahead.
With great power comes great responsibility — that's the iconic mantra that's been at the heart of Spider-Man since his introduction in 1962.
But in 2026, should that great power include the ability to run a mass surveillance program on the people of New York City, with nothing more than a quip to explain it?
If you go by the events of "Spider-Man: Brand New Day," in theaters now, in which Spider-Man (Tom Holland) uses illegal facial recognition technology to identify both Scorpion (Michael Mando), a criminal, and Jean Grey (Sadie Sink), a telepathic mutant running amok in NYC, the answer is yes.
The technology is remarkably similar to what Batman uses at the end of "The Dark Knight," released in 2008. Except in that film, using it was presented as a huge ethical dilemma, and it's ultimately destroyed.
It's been 18 years since "The Dark Knight." What does the treatment of surveillance in "Brand New Day" say about our attitudes toward it? They've changed.
Spider-Man's line 'speaks to the extreme extent to which people are surveilled right now'
Spider-Man reveals the technology when looking for Scorpion, telling Detective DeWolff (Liza Colón-Zayas) that he has "every camera in New York running a facial recognition scan."
"That sounds super illegal, Spider-Man," she responds. "I'm gonna pretend I didn't hear that."
He laughs and says it's "probably for the best."
Some Spider-Man fans were upset about Spidey's relaxed attitude toward the surveillance technology. On X and Reddit, they used nicknames like "Peter Thiel Parker" and "Palantir Parker" to describe the character.
Peter Thiel's Palantir Technologies provides government agencies, including ICE and the Department of Defense, with software such as Gotham. It "supports soldiers with an AI-powered kill chain" by integrating target identification and target effector pairing, among other capabilities, according to the company.
Nicholas Carnes, a political scientist, professor of public policy at Duke University, and co-editor of "The Politics of the Marvel Cinematic Universe," told Business Insider he was "very uncomfortable" with Spider-Man's illegal technology "being a throwaway line."
"I thought, my goodness, how blasé it seems to now say, 'Oh, I'm just going to do this. Don't tell on me, detective,'" Carnes said.
For Carnes, the nonchalance of the moment reflects how pervasive surveillance has become in our day-to-day lives. "That line can only exist in the movie in the way it does in a world where people are accustomed to being surveilled," he added.
The surveillance debate has shifted since 'The Dark Knight'
"The Dark Knight," released 18 years ago, approaches surveillance technology differently and shows just how far attitudes have shifted.
Bruce Wayne argues with his friend, Lucius Fox, about the implications of using surveillance tech on fellow citizens, leading Lucius to threaten to quit. The film climaxes with Bruce destroying the device, much to Lucius' relief.
The film was released in July 2008, near the end of George W. Bush's second term, when some Americans were concerned about the application of laws like the Patriot Act and the NSA spying on American citizens. A Gallup poll put Bush's approval rating at just 29% that summer.
Nearly two decades later, surveillance concerns haven't disappeared, but we've all gotten more accustomed to living with it in every part of our lives, including at home, at work, in our cars, and at school.
"Christian Bale was Batman in an era when people were getting really concerned about what's happening with their data. And Spider-Man is sort of surveilling the entire city in an era when people are being told a hundred times a day, 'AI is good, and it's your friend,'" Carnes said.
That's not to say "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" doesn't criticize government power. Carnes noted that the movie ultimately portrays government oversight in a negative light.
"This is a movie that really depicts a fictional department of the US government [the Department of Damage Control] as shadowy, abusive, unaccountable, and utterly immoral," Carnes said.
The film ends with Spider-Man breaking into a DODC facility and discovering the agency has been developing weapons specifically designed to take him down.
While Peter has regrets about creating technology that was used against Jean and could have catastrophic consequences for mutants in the future, he never reckons with becoming Big Brother himself.
Spider-Man's surveillance tech isn't so far removed from reality
The technology Spider-Man uses to fight crime — without any oversight — isn't unlike surveillance systems that are already in place today.
Automatic license plate readers (ALPRs), including those made by Flock Safety, are used by police departments across the country to search camera networks for vehicles of interest.
Proponents of the technology argue it could be a helpful tool in preventing crime, supporting victims, and aiding police work. Critics argue that the tech has accuracy problems, raises privacy concerns, and lacks reliable oversight.
For now, it seems Americans share critics' concerns. A March 2026 poll by the Center for Democracy and Technology found that 74% of respondents were "concerned about the privacy and security of their personal data that is held by the government."
That raises another question: whether seeing this kind of surveillance wielded casually by a trusted superhero — Spider-Man — can continue to normalize it.
But Carnes noted that audiences have accepted superheroes having technology that, in the real world, would not fly.
"We're OK with Spider-Man having that power because he's Peter Parker, and he's dear to us, and we trust him," he said. "We would not be OK with virtually anyone having that in the real world."

Terabytes worth of credentials, many belonging to the world’s biggest and most sensitive organizations, have been exposed in a supply-chain attack on LiteLLM, an open source tool that streamlines AI-driven software development. Microsoft, Amazon, Cisco, Samsung, and Salesforce are only a handful of the entities whose access secrets were exposed.
The revelation was posted on Tuesday and Wednesday by security firms CloudSEK and Hudson Rock. CloudSEK said it found cloud keys, repository tokens, SSH keys, Kubernetes secrets, package publishing credentials, environment variables, and AI provider keys that could allow attackers to gain access to more than 2,500 organizations.
40 minutes is all it takes
The credentials were extracted during a 40-minute window in March while the victims used compromised versions of LiteLLM downloaded from the package’s official location in the Python Package Index repository. Hudson Rock said it made the discovery after analyzing a 195TB file that it obtained. Neither firm identified the source of the information.
The LiteLLM compromise was the result of a previous supply-chain attack that infected the widely used vulnerability scanner Trivy. Other software infected in the campaign includes KICS and the Telnyx Python SDK. TeamPCP, a ramshackle but extremely capable gang largely made up of teenagers, took credit for the attack, and researchers have largely corroborated the claim.
“I’ve confirmed the data is legit, by the way, multiple victim orgs,” independent security researcher Kevin Beaumont said. “It contains a significant volume of sensitive content at orgs. It’s a massive supply chain breach due to poor AI security—not because AI is the threat, but teens can run circles around orgs obsessed with rushing out AI and poor DevOps security.”

Millions crowd cities to see Spain's first total solar eclipse in over a century
MEDINACELI, Spain — Millions of people crowded cloudless cities and towns in Spain on Wednesday in search of the best views of a total solar eclipse, when the alignment of the sun, moon and Earth briefly plunged parts of the planet into darkness.
The crowds brought lawn chairs and umbrellas as they eagerly awaited the celestial spectacle, which began early in the evening. As the sky darkened, gradually at first and then quickly, people broke into applause and cheered. It was the country's first total solar eclipse in more than a century.
"It's simply impossible to imagine," Rosa Celiberti, a language teacher who watched from Medinaceli, a Roman-era hilltop town in northeast Spain, said with tears in her eyes. "No matter how many photos or videos you've seen, nothing comes even close to what it actually feels like."
Across a wide band of northern and central Spain and Portugal, millions of people enjoyed some of mainland Europe's best views of the eclipse. It also passed over slivers of Greenland and Iceland.
Totality — when the moon completely covers the sun's light — was expected to last less than 2½ minutes, reaching its maximum duration off Iceland's west coast. By the time it got to a small patch of Portugal and then to Spain, just before sunset, totality dwindled to a minute or so. The total eclipse then ended over the Mediterranean.
The eclipse was expected to draw at least a half-million additional visitors, Spanish authorities said. Demand for hotel rooms along the path of totality, including in the northern cities of A Coruña, Bilbao and Santiago de Compostela, soared.
Rural areas prepared for an influx of visitors
The event unfolded against the backdrop of scorching summer temperatures and wildfires, and Spanish officials rolled out a large public safety campaign.
Temperatures across much of Spain climbed above 35 degrees Celsius (95 Fahrenheit) in many areas where the eclipse was observed. Some 350 official viewing sites were set up across the sparsely populated interior, and more than 33,500 law enforcement officers were deployed to observation areas and access points, the Interior Ministry said.
Only weeks ago, the most destructive wildfire in Spanish history devoured 500 square kilometers (193 square miles) and forced the evacuation of tens of thousands of people in Ávila, in central Spain. Several smaller wildfires remain active elsewhere in southern and central parts of the country.
Despite clouds, sky watchers in Iceland witnessed darkness
In Reykjavik, clouds did not prevent hundreds of people from gathering in bright raincoats in front of the landmark Hallgrímskirkja church as the skies darkened.
With rain falling, the disk of the sun was barely perceptible and then, suddenly, the lights went out. Only the glow of phones held aloft could be seen.
The crowd cheered the darkness as it rained harder and roared even louder when the first light returned. They did not wait to watch the remainder of the partial eclipse and quickly cleared out of the square.
Eclipse glasses sold fast
Special eclipse glasses were essential for safe viewing, even if only a sliver of the sun remained visible. The glasses are made with special filters that block solar radiation that can damage the eyes.
For months, supermarkets, department stores, museums and planetariums across Spain had sold or distributed the glasses, with many pharmacies running out of stock ahead of Wednesday.
On Tuesday evening in downtown Madrid, a long line formed outside a photo shop where a sign read, "We carry eclipse glasses."
One woman emerged triumphantly and reassured those waiting: "He has boxes and boxes of them!"
A ship circles waters near Greenland hoping to catch a glimpse
Sverre Rud, captain of the MS Spitsbergen, was circling the waters of Rypefjord in eastern Greenland trying to make sure he was perfectly positioned for his 126 passengers to view the spectacle. All day, people came up to Rud to ask if he had nailed the right spot, with no clouds.
"I will do my best," Rud said. "I will pull out my superman powers."
The eclipse may have been startling for the passengers, who had been experiencing 24 hours of daylight on a 17-day cruise in locations mostly north of the Arctic Circle.
Suddenly, for two minutes it was dark.
Even so, the mood on the polar ship had been pure anticipation.
"Everyone is very enthusiastic," Rud said. "When we were down for breakfast earlier, it was almost like a little bit of a Christmas Eve feeling here."
Hotel costs skyrocketed in Spain and Iceland
Rooms in Reykjavík, Iceland's capital, averaged more than $1,000 for Wednesday night as Icelanders prepared for their first total solar eclipse since 1954 and the first visible from the capital since 1433.
Prices were roughly double 2025 rates, according to data group Lighthouse Intelligence. Many tourists made bookings years in advance. But cloudy skies prevailed across much of the island.
Authorities expected up to 20,000 additional overseas visitors during an already busy peak tourist period. Iceland is home to fewer than 400,000 people.
The 70-room Hotel Keflavík in the Reykjanesbaer municipality was fully booked, with guests hoping to see around one minute and 45 seconds of totality.
"Eclipse time, of course, has been very demanding, and many people came to us early, like last year," said Steinþór Jónsson, the hotel's owner and manager.
Jónsson said he had seen nothing like it since 1986, the year the hotel opened, when U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev held a summit in Reykjavík.
"When I opened the hotel, we had Reagan and Gorbachev meeting. It was very hectic here," he said with a smile. "Besides Reagan and Gorbachev, the eclipse is the biggest."
Sun mostly obscured in Britain
Across Britain, where the sun was more than 90% obscured, people flocked to hilltop parks and anywhere with an open view of the sky to see the best eclipse since 1999.
In Greenwich Park, with views of the River Thames and central London, the sky turned an eerie gray as a sliver of light sat atop the moon like a hat.
Veronica Orozco popped open a bottle of champagne to share with neighbors as she witnessed the second eclipse of her life.
"I was in Venezuela and I was young and I thought that the sun would not come back. My dad said, 'It is science, of course it will come back,'" she recalled. "Now sitting here at the age of 41, it is still magical."
Aja Lilit, who turned 24 on Tuesday, said the eclipse was like a "birthday present from the universe."
She said the rare event made her think of how small she was at a "cosmic level."

As the CJP protests gathered momentum, a parallel campaign began online against some of the women who participated in them. Accounts targeting the protesters circulated their videos, hurled abuse at them and published screenshots containing sensitive personal information, turning online trolling into outright doxxing.
Many of those targeted had either spoken to the media during the protests or posted reels and other content on social media with abusive language against Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Several Right-wing handles subjected them to sustained trolling and abuse while putting their private information in the public domain.
The most alarming instance involved a young woman from Noida. A clip of her using expletives against Modi during the Delhi protests went viral, following which Delhi-based Supreme Court lawyer Smriti Singh Chandel filed a zero FIR against her, invoking charges of defamation and “intentional insult to provoke breach of peace”.
Chandel also posted a photo of the FIR complaint on her Instagram handle, which revealed the home address of the accused individual. She also posted a video of men outside Gautam Budh Nagar police station holding the complaint copy and claiming they had access to the personal details of the female. Police had “assured” them, they said, that she would be arrested within days.
Young Female Protester Bears The Brunt
Confusion over the female’s age — whether or not she is a minor — and her name further problematised the case. After Prime Minister Narendra Modi posted a video saying that he “forgave” everyone who had abused him during the protest, the female protester posted an apology video, admitting her mistake, apologising to him and to the country. She claimed she was “influenced” by others using abusive language against the PM.
As reports began to suggest that the protester was in fact a minor, responding to allegations of doxxing a minor, trolls claimed that the girl in the apology video was not the same as the girl in the viral video. Several Right-wing influencers took to X to claim that a minor girl was being used to cover up for the actual 25-year-old protester, so that POCSO cases could be registered. Some even claimed she was using her younger sister for sympathy while some users went to the length of comparing facial features to prove their point.
The case significantly blew up when mainstream media aired her alleged name and face on national television. Times Now amplified the claim that the protester was a 25-year-old woman named Ruchika Singh. NDTV’s Shiv Aroor made the same claim, showing her face and revealing her identity.
CNN-News18 also made the same claim, while exposing her face; the channel on July 31 reported how they have “tracked down” the girl to her society complex in Noida, from where she had reportedly absconded. Citing repeated visits from the police as well as from strangers, the single mother-daughter duo reportedly had to leave their rented accommodation and shift elsewhere.
To make matters worse, on July 31, CNN-News 18 also claimed to have gained access to “exclusive voices” from the female protesters life that “nobody else has”. In an outright case of breach of privacy, a reporter from the organisation reached the “beauty salon” where the girl had allegedly learnt nail art till the month of June.
The reporter speaks at length with the owner of the nail salon, probing over the girl’s association with the salon. The owner mentions that the her name was not Ruchika Singh, as was being claimed by the media. He also claimed that on repeated failures to furnish her identity details, specifically her Aadhaar Card, the girl was reportedly asked by the management to not come back.
In an interview with ABP News, the victim of this doxxing episode clarified that her name is not Ruchika Singh and neither is she 25 years old.
The girl, who stated her age to be 15, reportedly faced constant harassment and threats from people in the neighbourhood, including threats of “murder and rape“. The mother, who also appears in the ABP interview, urges the public to stop the relentless abuse against her daughter.
The mother stated that despite the “PM forgiving her (daughter)”, an army of anti-social elements and police were repeatedly visiting their residence, which they were eventually forced to vacate given the increasing threat to their privacy and survival. “What will you get from harassing a child?” the mother asked, while extending gradtitude to Modi for granting her daughter “jeevandaan”. She repeatedly implores Modi and the masses to “let them live in peace and return to their home”.
Notably, Chandel, by her own admission, had “learnt” about the young girl’s name and details from social media users. The police complaint as well as the FIR went on to mention her as 25-year-old while the girl and her mother maintained that she is 15. “There are people claiming that it is her younger sister who has made the apology; they are saying I have hidden my daughter. This is bizarre; why would any mother throw her child into this vicious cycle of threats?” the mother said to The Print.
‘Arrest These Women’: Online Mob Justice
This was not an isolated incident. Several Right-wing accounts on X were determined to identify and locate female protesters. Retired IAS officer Sanjay Dixit, who runs the Hindutva propaganda page Jaipur Dialogues, specifically targeted women protesters who had allegedly abused Modi. In one of his posts, he shared a collage of twelve such women, urging the Delhi Police to “arrest them”.

A new survey in Arunachal Pradesh has documented recurring experiences of widespread harassment of members of the LGBTQIA+ community in the State.
Also read | On India’s rainbow trail | Queer-focused walks are finding an audience in the country
According to the Itanagar-based HimKai Research Institute (HRI), the pestering or provocation has led to identity concealment, discrimination-related distress, and low confidence in institutional protection among the LGBTQIA+ respondents in the State.
LGBTQIA+ expands to Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, Queer or Questioning, Intersex, and Asexual.
The HRI conducted the anonymous online survey between June 2 and August 2. It received 62 submissions, one of which was excluded during geographic eligibility and data-quality screening because the self-reported home district could not be mapped in Arunachal Pradesh.
“Among the 61 respondents included in the analysis, 49.2% said they hid their gender identity or sexual orientation most of the time or always because of fear of discrimination or violence. Half of valid respondents said they felt accepted within their family rarely or never, while 44.3% said they felt safe in their local community rarely or never,” the HRI report said.
“Experiences of harassment and discrimination were reported across several settings. Some 91.8% of respondents reported verbal harassment at least rarely, while 52.5% reported physical threats or violence at least rarely. Among valid responses, 85.0% reported discrimination in school or college at least rarely, and 63.2% reported workplace discrimination,” it said.
The survey also found that 72.9% of valid respondents felt compelled to change their behaviour or appearance sometimes or more often to retain work or education. A further 57.9% said their identity affected access to employment or income opportunities at least rarely.
Religious, cultural exclusion
“Mental wellbeing emerged as a significant concern. Among valid responses, 76.7% reported experiencing stress, anxiety or emotional distress related to discrimination sometimes or more often, including 48.3% who experienced it most of the time or always. Access to mental-health or peer support was uneven: 41.0% said such support was available most of the time or always, while 36.1% said it was available rarely or never,” the report said.
The findings also point to a gap between awareness of rights and confidence in institutions. While 56.7% of valid respondents agreed that they were aware of their legal rights, 63.3% disagreed that laws and policies adequately protect LGBTQIA+ persons, and 66.7% disagreed that police and authorities respond sensitively to LGBTQIA+ issues.
Religion, culture and social belonging received particularly cautious assessments. Some 72.1% did not agree that religion or faith practices are accepting of LGBTQIA+ persons. More than half disagreed that their identity is compatible with their cultural or tribal background or that local traditions allow space for diverse identities, with 51.7% of valid respondents disagreeing that they feel a sense of belonging in society.
Healthcare emerged as a comparatively more positive area. Among valid respondents, 56.7% said that they felt comfortable accessing healthcare most of the time or always, and 75.0% said healthcare providers treated them with respect most of the time or always.
“Friends were the most frequently reported source of support, mentioned by 37 respondents, followed by LGBTQIA+ networks, mentioned by 12.
Six respondents mentioned. Awareness and sensitisation were the most common single priority identified for improving LGBTQIA+ lives in Arunachal Pradesh, followed by legal protection,” the report said.
HRI director Ranju Dodum said the study was intended to begin building locally grounded evidence on experiences that are often discussed without adequate data.
“LGBTQIA+ experiences in Arunachal Pradesh cannot simply be assumed from national conversations. Family, community, tribal identity, religion, education and employment all shape how people experience acceptance and safety here. This is a baseline study and its numbers must be read with methodological caution, but they point to questions that deserve deeper research and serious public discussion,” he said.
The report recommends sustained sensitisation programmes in schools, colleges, workplaces, healthcare institutions, police and public administration; confidential mechanisms for reporting discrimination; stronger mental-health and peer-support systems; safe community spaces; more inclusive education and workplace practices; and locally grounded engagement with families, community institutions and faith leaders.
The survey sample was predominantly young, with 90.2% of respondents between 18 and 35 years.
